title: Refraction: the rule of the bend, and how light gets trapped

summary.text: Shine a torch at a slant into water and the beam turns toward an upright line. Shine it straight on and it does not turn at all. Your child measures the bend with a protractor and finds the pattern. The same rule explains why a diamond sparkles, why a fish sees the whole sky in one round window, and how hair-thin glass fibres carry the internet. It also explains why a hot road looks wet, how two lenses make a telescope, and how spectacles work, which nobody could explain for hundreds of years after people began wearing them.
summary.art: A rectangular tank of milky water on white paper with a torch beam entering at a slant and turning toward a dotted upright line, and a protractor lying beside it.

intro.hook: A fish looks up at you from under the water. Above her, the whole sky, from one edge to the other, is squeezed into one round window. Outside that window she sees only a silver ceiling. Why?
intro.text: You already know that light bends when it goes from air into water. Now we ask by how much, and what happens when you push the bend as far as it will go. You will measure the bend with a torch and a protractor. Then you will find out how the same rule makes a silver ceiling under the water, a glowing stream of water, a sparkling diamond and the cables that carry phone calls under the sea.
intro.art: A view from under the water, looking up: a bright round window of blue sky with a boat in the middle, and a silver ring around it showing the seabed.

outcomes: I can name the parts of a bend diagram: the surface, the normal line, the angle in and the angle out.
I can say the rule of the bend: light bends toward the normal when it slows down, away from it when it speeds up, and not at all when it arrives straight on.
I can measure how much a beam turns in water with a protractor, say how sure I am of my numbers, and finish the test like a scientist: what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that a bigger refractive index means slower light and a bigger bend, and that this is not the same as being heavier.
I can explain total internal reflection: why light inside water or glass bounces back when it hits the surface at a shallow angle.
I can use total internal reflection to explain a fish's round window, a glowing water jet, a sparkling diamond and an optical fibre.
I can explain a hot-road mirage as light bending a little at a time through layers of air.
I can explain how hollow and bulging lenses fix short sight and long sight, and how two lenses make a telescope.

terms.meaning: An imaginary straight line at a right angle to a surface, at the spot where light arrives. Scientists measure the bend of light from this line, not from the surface.
terms.example: Stand a pencil straight up on a flat table. The pencil shows the normal line for the table top.
terms.art: A flat water surface with a dotted line standing straight up from it at the spot where a light ray arrives.

terms.meaning: The amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. A wide turn is a big angle and a small turn is a small angle.
terms.example: The corner of a book is an angle. The hands of a clock make a different angle every minute.
terms.art: Two lines meeting at a point with a curved arrow between them.

terms.meaning: The unit we use to measure an angle. A square corner is 90 degrees. A full turn all the way round is 360 degrees.
terms.example: A protractor is a ruler for angles. It has the degrees marked along its curved edge.
terms.art: A half-circle protractor with marks at 0, 30, 60 and 90 degrees.

terms.meaning: A thin, straight path of light, drawn as a line with an arrow on it. A ray shows which way light is going.
terms.example: A torch with a very thin slit in front of it sends out something close to a single ray.
terms.art: A torch with a black card over its front, sending a thin straight beam.

terms.meaning: The angle between the ray arriving at a surface and the normal line. Scientists call it the angle of incidence.
terms.example: A torch pointed straight down at a table has an angle in of 0 degrees. A torch lying nearly flat has an angle in close to 90 degrees.
terms.art: A ray coming down to a surface from the upper left, with the angle to the normal marked in blue.

terms.meaning: The angle between the ray after it has crossed the surface and the normal line. Scientists call it the angle of refraction.
terms.example: A beam that meets the water at 60 degrees from the normal carries on inside the water at about 40 degrees from the normal. That 40 degrees is the angle out.
terms.art: A ray crossing into water and bending toward the normal, with the angle on the water side marked in orange.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how many times slower light travels in a material than in empty space. A bigger number means slower light and a bigger bend.
terms.example: Water is about 1.33 and glass about 1.5. Diamond is about 2.4, so diamond slows light the most of these three.
terms.art: A row of four blocks labelled air, water, glass and diamond, with a longer arrow in air and a shorter arrow in diamond.

terms.meaning: What happens when light inside water or glass reaches the surface at a very shallow angle. None of it gets out. All of it bounces back inside, like off a mirror.
terms.example: Under the water, look up at the surface from a low angle. It shines silver, like a mirror.
terms.art: A ray inside a block of glass hitting the top surface at a shallow angle and bouncing back down, with no light escaping.

terms.meaning: The angle from the normal beyond which light inside a material is trapped. For water it is about 49 degrees. For glass it is about 42 degrees. For diamond it is about 24 degrees.
terms.example: A diamond has a small critical angle, so it traps light easily. That is part of why a diamond sparkles.
terms.art: Three rays inside water: one leaving, one just skimming the surface, and one bouncing back, with the middle one marked critical angle.

terms.meaning: A strand of very clear glass or plastic about as thin as a hair. It carries light along its length, even round bends, by trapping the light inside.
terms.example: Internet cables under the sea are bundles of optical fibres. Doctors also use fibres to see inside the body.
terms.art: A hair-thin glass strand curving in a loop with a ray of light zigzagging along inside it.

terms.meaning: A block of glass or clear plastic with flat sides that are not parallel. A common prism is shaped like a triangle. It turns a beam of light.
terms.example: A triangle-shaped glass prism turns a beam of sunlight and spreads it into a band of colours.
terms.art: A triangular glass prism with a ray entering one side and leaving the other turned toward its base.

terms.meaning: A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. It spreads light out. Scientists call it a concave lens.
terms.example: Spectacles for short sight use hollow lenses. Through them, the world looks a little smaller.
terms.art: Side view of a lens thin in the middle and thick at the edges, with parallel rays spreading apart after it.

terms.meaning: The spot where a bulging lens brings light from a faraway thing together. The distance from the lens to that spot is called its focal length.
terms.example: A magnifying glass held up to a window brings the window's light to a sharp picture on a card, at one distance only.
terms.art: A bulging lens with parallel rays bending to meet at one point, with a ruler showing the distance to that point.

terms.meaning: The unit for the strength of a lens. A lens with a focal length of 1 metre has a power of 1 dioptre. A shorter focal length means more dioptres and a stronger lens.
terms.example: Reading spectacles marked plus 2 have a focal length of half a metre, which is 50 centimetres.
terms.art: A pair of reading spectacles with the number plus 2 written on the arm.

terms.meaning: An eye problem where faraway things look blurry but close things look clear. The eye bends light a little too much, so the sharp picture forms in front of the back of the eye. Scientists call it myopia.
terms.example: A child who cannot read the board from the back of the class, but reads a book easily, may be short-sighted.
terms.art: A side view of an eye where the rays from a faraway tree meet in front of the back of the eye and spread out again.

terms.meaning: An eye problem where close things look blurry. The eye cannot bend light enough for near things, so the sharp picture would form behind the back of the eye. Many older people need reading spectacles for this.
terms.example: A grandparent who holds the newspaper at arm's length to read it may be long-sighted.
terms.art: A side view of an eye where the rays from a nearby book would meet behind the back of the eye.

terms.meaning: The layer at the back of the eye where the picture forms. It turns light into signals that travel to the brain.
terms.example: When you look at a tree, a tiny upside-down picture of the tree forms on your retina.
terms.art: A cut-open eye with a tiny upside-down tree glowing on the back wall.

terms.meaning: A tube with lenses or mirrors that makes faraway things look closer and bigger.
terms.example: A telescope shows the craters on the Moon and the four biggest moons of Jupiter.
terms.art: A long tube on a tripod pointing at the Moon, with a child's eye at the small end.

terms.meaning: A picture of the sky, or of faraway things, that appears near the ground. It is made when light bends a little at a time through layers of hot and cool air. A mirage is real light. A camera can photograph it.
terms.example: On a hot day, a long straight road ahead can look wet and shiny. The shine is a picture of the sky.
terms.art: A long hot road shimmering in the distance with a shiny patch that mirrors the sky and a far lorry upside down in it.

terms.meaning: Lines that run side by side and always stay the same distance apart, so they never meet.
terms.example: The two rails of a railway track are parallel.
terms.art: Two railway rails running side by side into the distance.

explanations.concept: The rule of the bend: toward the normal, or away
explanations.definition: When light slows down as it crosses into a new material at a slant, it bends toward the normal line. When light speeds up as it crosses out, it bends away from the normal line. Light that arrives straight on, along the normal, does not bend at all.
explanations.description: Draw a line standing straight up from the surface, at the spot where the light arrives. This is the normal. Now measure the angle between the ray and the normal, in degrees. Going from air into water, the ray bends toward the normal, so the angle in the water is smaller than the angle in the air. Going from water back into air, the ray bends away from the normal, so the angle in the air is bigger. The bigger the slant, the bigger the bend. A beam at 60 degrees in the air goes on at about 41 degrees in the water, so it turns by about 19 degrees. A beam at 20 degrees turns by only about 5. A beam at 0 degrees does not turn at all. Glass bends light more than water does, and diamond bends it more still. But the rule is always the same: into a slower material, toward the normal. Out into a faster material, away from it. Light paths can also be run backwards. A ray that goes from air to water follows exactly the same path if it is sent back from the water to the air.
examples: A torch beam going into a tank of water at a slant turns toward the upright line, and the angle in the water is smaller than the angle in the air.
A beam of sunlight going into a glass of water turns downward and steeper than it arrived.
A beam that goes straight down into a pond, along the normal, goes on straight down.
explanations.art: A water surface with a dotted normal line, a ray coming in from the upper left at 60 degrees and bending to 41 degrees below the surface, with both angles marked.
explanations.context: This card explains the main rule of this unit: which way light bends when it crosses from one material into another, and by how much.

explanations.concept: How much slower: the refractive index
explanations.definition: The refractive index of a material is a number that tells how many times slower light moves there than in empty space. The bigger the number, the slower the light and the bigger the bend.
explanations.description: In empty space, light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. Air slows light by a tiny amount, so for air the number is almost exactly 1. Water has a refractive index of about 1.33. That means light in water moves 1.33 times slower than in empty space, which is about 225,000 kilometres a second. Cooking oil is about 1.47. Glass is about 1.5, though the exact number depends on the kind of glass. Diamond is about 2.4, so light in a diamond moves at less than half its speed in air. Notice something odd. Oil floats on water, so oil is lighter for its size, yet oil bends light more. So a bigger refractive index does not mean heavier. It depends on how the atoms of the material hold on to their electrons, and how the electrons react to the light passing by. This is why a clear glass marble almost vanishes in honey or oil, which have refractive indexes near that of glass. Where two see-through materials have the same number, light does not bend between them.
examples: Light in water travels at about three quarters of its speed in air, because 1 divided by 1.33 is about three quarters.
Cooking oil bends light more than water, although oil floats on water.
Glass bends light more than water does, and diamond bends it more than glass. The order from least to most bending is air, water, oil, glass, diamond.
explanations.art: A bar chart with bars for air 1, water 1.33, oil 1.47, glass 1.5 and diamond 2.4, with a speed arrow getting shorter beside each bar.
explanations.context: This card explains the number that tells how strongly a material bends light, and why it is not the same as how heavy the material is.

explanations.concept: A glass block shifts a beam, and a prism turns it
explanations.definition: A block of glass with parallel sides bends a ray toward the normal on the way in, and away from it by the same amount on the way out. So the ray leaves parallel to the way it arrived, but shifted sideways. A prism has sides that are not parallel, so it turns the ray for good.
explanations.description: Send a ray at a slant into a thick glass slab. At the first surface it bends toward the normal. Inside the glass it goes straight. At the second surface, which is parallel to the first, the normals are parallel too. Now the ray bends away from the normal by exactly the same amount, so it comes out going in the same direction as before. But it has been moved sideways a little. That is why a thick window can make the view outside look slightly shifted when you look at a slant. A prism is different. Its two surfaces are tilted toward each other, so the second bend adds to the first instead of undoing it. The ray leaves turned toward the thick end of the prism. A bulging lens is like a set of prisms, thin at the top and bottom, and the prisms turn the rays toward each other. Isaac Newton used prisms in 1666 and showed that each colour in sunlight bends by a slightly different amount.
examples: Look at a pencil through the side of a thick, clean glass block at a slant. The pencil seems shifted sideways.
A triangle-shaped prism turns a torch beam toward its thick end.
Two prisms placed base to base act like a bulging lens, and bring two rays together.
explanations.art: A ray going through a rectangular glass block and coming out parallel to the first ray but shifted sideways, next to a triangular prism turning a ray toward its base.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens to light that goes in one side of a block of glass and out of the other, and how a prism is different.

explanations.concept: The fish's round window and the silver ceiling: total internal reflection
explanations.definition: When light inside water reaches the surface at more than about 49 degrees from the normal, none of it gets out. All of it bounces back down, like off a mirror. This is called total internal reflection.
explanations.description: Light going from water into air bends away from the normal. The bigger the angle in the water, the bigger the angle in the air, and the faster it grows. At an angle of about 49 degrees in the water, the ray in the air would have to lie flat along the surface, at 90 degrees. Beyond that angle, there is no way out. Scientists call 49 degrees the critical angle for water. Every bit of the light bounces back into the water, and the surface works like a perfect mirror. Now picture a fish looking up. Rays from the whole sky, from one horizon to the other, are bent down by the surface into a cone about 97 degrees wide. So the fish sees the entire sky squeezed into one round window straight above her. Outside the window, she is looking at the underside of the surface at shallow angles. There it is a mirror, and it shows the seabed. A diver sees the same. This only works when the light is going from a slower material to a faster one. Light going from air into water can never be trapped.
examples: Hold a glass of water above your eyes and look up through the side at the surface. At a slant, the surface turns silver.
A diver looking up on a calm day sees a bright round window of sky with a silver ring around it.
Light inside a diamond that hits the outside at a shallow angle bounces back inside, instead of escaping.
explanations.art: A fish under water with a cone of light from the whole sky narrowing to her eye, and a silver ring around the round window showing the pebbles below.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens when light inside water meets the surface at a very shallow angle, and why the surface becomes a mirror.

explanations.concept: Light trapped on purpose: water jets, diamonds and optical fibres
explanations.definition: Total internal reflection can trap light inside a clear material. It can then be guided along a curve, as in a stream of water or an optical fibre, or kept bouncing inside a gem so that it comes out sparkling.
explanations.description: In the 1840s, Jean-Daniel Colladon in Geneva showed that light shone into a jet of water from a tank follows the jet as it curves down. Each time the light reaches the edge of the jet, the angle is shallow, so it bounces back in. The jet glows like a bent pipe of light. An optical fibre does the same inside a strand of glass thinner than a pencil lead, about as thin as a human hair. The glass has a thin coat with a lower refractive index, so light bounces from wall to wall along the strand, even round bends. In 1966, Charles Kao and George Hockham argued that glass of that time dimmed light because of impurities, not because glass itself blocks light. Purer glass could carry light for kilometres. Kao shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009. The Indian-born physicist Narinder Singh Kapany did early work on bundles of fibres in the 1950s and is often called the father of fibre optics. Today most of the data between continents crosses the oceans as flashes of light inside fibres on the sea floor. A diamond has a very small critical angle, about 24 degrees, so it traps light easily. A diamond cutter cuts the sides at angles chosen to send the light back out through the top, so the stone flashes.
examples: A glowing jet of water from a bottle in a dark room carries a torch beam along its curve.
Doctors use bundles of optical fibres to look inside the body through a tiny cut.
Cables under the sea carry phone calls and internet between countries as flashes of light.
explanations.art: A jet of water curving down from a bottle in a dark room, glowing along its whole length, next to a cut-open optical fibre with a ray zigzagging inside.
explanations.context: This card is about using trapped light: guiding it round bends in water and glass, and making diamonds sparkle.

explanations.concept: Mirages and shimmering roads: bending a little at a time
explanations.definition: Air that is hotter is thinner, and light moves slightly faster in it. On a hot day, light from the sky bends gradually as it passes down through layers of air that get hotter nearer the road, and curves back up to your eyes. You see a picture of the sky on the road, which looks like water.
explanations.description: Near a sun-baked road the air touching the ground is much hotter than the air higher up. Hot air is thinner, so light travels through it a tiny bit faster. A ray heading down toward the road meets thinner and thinner air. The lower side of the ray moves a little faster than the upper side, so the whole ray swings upward, a little at a time, until it curves up toward your eye. Your brain follows the light straight back and puts the sky down on the road. That is why the shiny patch looks like water. It is real light, and a camera can photograph it. If you walk toward the patch, it keeps moving away, because it is only visible from a shallow angle. The same bending also makes the air above a hot tava shimmer, and makes stars twinkle. Over very cold sea, the opposite happens. Light curves down, and a ship beyond the horizon can seem to float in the sky. Sailors have long reported these pictures, which are sometimes called the fata morgana.
examples: A long highway in the afternoon looks wet far ahead, and the wetness is a picture of the sky.
In the Thar desert, travellers see shining lakes in the distance that vanish as they come closer.
The air above a hot roof or a hot tava shimmers, and the view through it wobbles.
explanations.art: A hot road at noon with a curved ray from the sky bending up to a child's eye and a shiny patch on the road where the child seems to see water.
explanations.context: This card explains the mirage, the shiny patch on a hot road, as an example of light bending a little at a time through layers of air.

explanations.concept: Lenses in detail: bulging lenses, hollow lenses and the focus
explanations.definition: A bulging lens bends rays toward each other so that rays from a faraway thing meet at one spot, the focus point. A hollow lens bends rays away from each other. A fatter bulging lens has a shorter focal length.
explanations.description: Think of a lens as a set of prisms. In a bulging lens the prisms are thick at the middle and thin at the edge. Every ray bends toward the thick part, and rays that are further from the middle bend more. Because of this, parallel rays from a faraway thing all arrive at the same spot, which is the focus point. The distance from the lens to that spot is the focal length. A fatter, more curved lens bends rays more sharply, so its focus point is closer. Lens strength is measured in dioptres. One divided by the focal length in metres gives the power in dioptres. So a lens with a focal length of 50 centimetres has a power of 2 dioptres. A hollow lens is thin in the middle, so its prisms turn the rays away from each other. The rays never meet, so a hollow lens cannot throw a picture on a card. It makes things look smaller. You can tell which kind of lens you hold. Look at some print through it. If the print looks bigger, the lens is bulging. If it looks smaller, the lens is hollow.
examples: A magnifying glass has a short focal length. Reading spectacles for a grandparent have a longer one, such as 50 centimetres.
Spectacles for a short-sighted child make the print look smaller, so they are hollow lenses.
A peephole in a door has a hollow lens that shows a wide, small view of the person outside.
explanations.art: Two side views: a bulging lens bringing parallel rays to a focus point with the focal length marked, and a hollow lens spreading parallel rays apart with dotted lines tracing back to a point.
explanations.context: This card explains the two kinds of lens, what the focus point is, and how lens strength is measured.

explanations.concept: The eye is a lens: short sight, long sight and spectacles
explanations.definition: Your eye bends light to make a sharp picture on the retina. In short sight the eye bends light too much, so the picture forms in front of the retina. In long sight it forms behind. Spectacles with a hollow or bulging lens move the picture to the right place.
explanations.description: Most of the bending in your eye is done at its clear front window, the cornea. The lens inside does the fine focusing. It gets fatter for near things and thinner for far things. For a sharp picture, the light must come to a point exactly on the retina. In short sight, the eyeball is a little too long, or the eye bends light too much. Rays from far things meet before the retina and spread out again, so the picture is blurry. A hollow lens in front of the eye spreads the rays a little first, which moves the focus back onto the retina. In long sight, the eyeball is a little too short, or the lens cannot get fat enough. Near things focus behind the retina. A bulging lens helps. Around the age of forty or fifty, the lens inside everyone's eyes gets stiffer, which makes close reading hard, and reading spectacles help. Studies suggest that children who spend more time outdoors in daylight are less likely to become short-sighted, and scientists are still working out why. Wearing the right spectacles does not make eyes weaker. Health organisations report that millions of people in India and across the world need spectacles and do not have them. When the lens inside the eye turns cloudy, which is called a cataract, a surgeon can replace it with a clear plastic lens. The Aravind Eye Hospital in Madurai, started in 1976, is known for doing this operation for very large numbers of people, many of them free of charge.
examples: A short-sighted child sees the board blurry but reads a book easily, and a hollow lens in spectacles makes the board clear.
A grandparent holds the newspaper far away to read it until reading spectacles with a bulging lens bring the print back into focus.
A cloudy eye lens can be replaced with a clear plastic one in a short operation.
explanations.art: Two side views of an eye with rays from a faraway tree: one with the focus in front of the retina and a hollow lens in front, and one with a bulging lens fixing a focus behind the retina.
explanations.context: This card explains how the eye makes a sharp picture, and how spectacles fix short sight and long sight.

explanations.concept: Two lenses make a telescope or a microscope
explanations.definition: A telescope has a large weak lens that makes a small picture of a faraway thing, and a small strong lens that magnifies that picture. To find how many times the telescope magnifies, divide the focal length of the first lens by the focal length of the second. A microscope uses two strong lenses in the same way for tiny things close by.
explanations.description: A single bulging lens makes a picture of the faraway thing at its focus point. The picture is small and upside down. Now put a second lens, a strong magnifier, so that you look at that small picture. The magnifier makes it look big. The first lens is the objective lens. The second is the eyepiece. If the objective has a focal length of 60 centimetres and the eyepiece has a focal length of 6 centimetres, the telescope magnifies 10 times, because 60 divided by 6 is 10. This kind of telescope shows everything upside down. Galileo built telescopes in 1609 and by 1610 had seen mountains on the Moon, many more stars and four moons circling Jupiter. A microscope is built the same way, but the first lens is a very strong one held close to a tiny thing, so that it makes a large picture, and the eyepiece magnifies that picture again. Robert Hooke used a microscope with two lenses, and in 1665 published drawings of what he saw, including the little boxes in cork that he called cells. Today the biggest telescopes use curved mirrors instead of lenses for the first step. Mirrors are easier to make large.
examples: A simple toy telescope with two lenses shows a far signboard upside down.
A school microscope uses two lenses to make a pond-water creature look hundreds of times bigger.
Binoculars have two telescopes, with prisms inside that turn the picture right way up.
explanations.art: A long tube with a large lens at the front and a small lens at the eye end, with rays from a far tree meeting inside the tube to make a small upside-down picture.
explanations.context: This card explains how using two lenses together magnifies far more than one lens can, in telescopes and microscopes.

explanations.concept: Rainbows: every raindrop is a tiny lens and mirror
explanations.definition: A rainbow is sunlight that has bent as it entered each raindrop, bounced off the back of the drop, and bent again on the way out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the colours leave the drop in slightly different directions.
explanations.description: A raindrop is a tiny round lens. Sunlight enters the drop and bends. Some of it bounces off the back of the drop, like off a weak mirror. This is not total internal reflection, where all the light bounces back. Here only part of the light bounces back, which is why rainbows are fairly faint. Then the light bends again as it leaves the drop. Red leaves at an angle of about 42 degrees from the line pointing away from the Sun. Violet leaves at about 40 degrees. Every drop at the same angle from that line sends the same colour to your eye. So the drops make a circle of each colour around the point opposite the Sun. You see the rainbow only with the Sun behind you. No two people see exactly the same rainbow, because each person's eyes are at a different place and so get light from different drops. In a second rainbow, which is higher and fainter, the light bounces twice inside each drop, and the colours are in the opposite order. From an aeroplane, a rainbow can be seen as a full circle. In the early 1300s, Theodoric of Freiberg in Germany and Kamal al-Din al-Farisi in Persia each worked out, by experiments with glass balls filled with water, that this is how rainbows are made.
examples: A garden sprinkler on a sunny day makes a small rainbow when you stand with the Sun behind you.
The fainter second rainbow outside a bright one has its colours in the opposite order.
A glass ball filled with water in a window throws bands of colour on the wall.
explanations.art: A single raindrop with a sunbeam entering at the left, bending, bouncing off the back and leaving at the left again with red and violet fanning out, and a child with the Sun behind them.
explanations.context: This card explains how bending and bouncing light together make a rainbow.

explanations.description: Telescopes appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, but nobody is sure who made the first one. The earliest records are patent applications, not proof of who thought of it first. Galileo did not invent the telescope, but he made the first well-known use of it for studying the sky.
examples: Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle maker in the town of Middelburg, asked for a patent for a telescope in October 1608.
A few weeks later, Jacob Metius of Alkmaar also asked for a patent.
Galileo heard of the new invention in 1609, made his own better one, and pointed it at the sky.

perspectives.explanation: His request for a patent in October 1608 is the first written record. The authorities did not grant it, because others seemed to know the secret too, but they paid him to make some telescopes.
He asked for a patent a few weeks after Lipperhey and said he had been working on the idea for two years. He also did not get a patent.
Later writers said that Janssen, another spectacle maker in the same town, had made the first one even earlier. The evidence is weak and historians doubt it.

He did not invent it, but he learned of it, built better ones by 1609, and was the first to use telescopes for careful study of the Moon, Jupiter and the stars. He made a telescope that magnified about 20 times.

explanations.art: Four small portraits in a row, a Dutch spectacle maker with a short tube, a second Dutchman with papers, a third at a workbench with lenses, and an Italian scholar looking at the Moon through a long tube.
explanations.context: This card is about the argument over who made the first telescope, which historians have not settled.

explanations.concept: Slowing light to a walking pace
explanations.definition: Light slows down in every material, and in 1999 a team led by Lene Hau at Harvard University in the USA slowed light to about 17 metres per second in a cloud of very cold atoms. That is about the speed of a cyclist.
explanations.description: In glass, light moves at about two thirds of its speed in air. That is a large change, but it is still very fast. Lene Vestergaard Hau, a physicist born in Denmark, and her team wanted to see how slow they could make it. They cooled a cloud of sodium atoms to a temperature a tiny fraction of a degree above the coldest possible, and shone a special laser through it. In the cloud, light that normally covers 300,000 kilometres in a second slowed to about 17 metres in a second. In 2001, her team and another team in the USA went further. They stopped a pulse of light inside a cloud of atoms and let it go again, a bit like pressing pause. Nobody yet knows if this will lead to everyday machines. Some scientists hope it might help store and send information in future quantum computers, but this is still only an idea.
examples: In the 1999 experiment, light slowed to about the speed of a person on a bicycle.
In 2001, a pulse of light was stopped inside a cloud of atoms and then released.
In ordinary glass, light slows only to about two thirds of its speed in air.
explanations.art: A glowing cloud of cold atoms in a glass cell, a pulse of light entering from the left as a long stretched ribbon and getting squashed and slow inside, with a cyclist drawn beside it for comparison.
explanations.context: This card is about experiments in which light was slowed to the speed of a bicycle.

agreed.text: Light bends toward the normal when it goes at a slant into a material where it moves more slowly, and away from the normal when it goes into a material where it moves faster.
agreed.evidence: The angles have been measured for about a thousand years, and anyone can check them with a torch, water and a protractor. Léon Foucault and others measured the speed of light in water directly in 1850, and found it slower than in air.

agreed.text: Light that arrives straight on, along the normal, does not bend.
agreed.evidence: A beam shone straight down into a tank goes on straight down. Every careful test gives the same result.

agreed.text: Light going from water into air at an angle bigger than about 49 degrees from the normal does not leave the water. It all bounces back.
agreed.evidence: Look up at the underside of the surface of a glass of water. At a shallow angle it turns silver like a mirror. Divers and photographers see a round window of sky with a silver ring around it.

agreed.text: Optical fibres carry light along their length by total internal reflection, and nearly all the data that crosses the oceans now travels this way.
agreed.evidence: Fibres have been made, tested and laid on the sea floor for decades. Charles Kao shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009 for his part in making this possible.

agreed.text: A mirage on a hot road is real light that has been bent, and not a trick of the mind.
agreed.evidence: Cameras photograph mirages. In pictures of a road mirage, the shiny patch really does show an upside-down image of the sky or of far objects.

agreed.text: Two lenses together can magnify far more than one lens, and a telescope magnifies by the ratio of the two focal lengths.
agreed.evidence: You can build a telescope with two lenses, measure each focal length and check how much bigger things look. Telescope makers have used this rule for four hundred years.

challenging.claim: A denser material always bends light more.
challenging.who: Many people, because a heavier material feels like it puts more stuff in the light's way.
challenging.for: Glass is heavier than water and bends light more than water does. Diamond is heavier still and bends light the most.
challenging.against: Cooking oil floats on water, so it is lighter for its size, yet it bends light more than water does. What matters is how the atoms of the material react to light, and not how heavy it is.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that heavier materials bend light more, and a simple fact that shows it is wrong.

challenging.claim: The silver ceiling under the water is a mirror coating that the water makes.
challenging.who: Some children, because it looks like a mirror.
challenging.for: It really does shine like a mirror, and you can see your finger in it.
challenging.against: There is no coating. It happens only when light inside the water meets the surface at a shallow angle. Look up steeply and the same surface is a clear window. So the surface is a mirror or a window, depending on the angle.
challenging.context: This card is about the silver surface seen from under the water, and what causes it.

challenging.claim: A mirage is something the mind makes up, not something real.
challenging.who: A common idea, because a mirage seems to disappear when you reach it.
challenging.for: A traveller cannot walk to the 'water'. It always stays ahead.
challenging.against: A camera can photograph a mirage. The picture of the sky on the road is made of real light that really has been bent. Our brain misreads where that light came from. The light is real. Only our guess about where it came from is wrong.
challenging.context: This card is about the common idea that a mirage is only imagined.

challenging.claim: All lenses make things look bigger.
challenging.who: People who have only used magnifying glasses.
challenging.for: Magnifying glasses, binoculars and microscopes all make things look bigger.
challenging.against: A hollow lens spreads light out and makes things look smaller. Spectacles for short sight and the peephole in a door are hollow lenses.
challenging.context: This card is about lenses that make things look smaller rather than bigger.

challenging.claim: Wearing spectacles makes your eyes weaker, so you should avoid them as long as you can.
challenging.who: A belief heard in many families.
challenging.for: People who get spectacles often seem to need stronger ones every few years.
challenging.against: Studies do not show that the right spectacles weaken eyes. Short sight tends to change while a child grows, because the eyeball grows too. Not wearing spectacles can make children struggle at school and, in some cases, can stop the eyes developing properly.
challenging.context: This card is about a common worry that spectacles harm the eyes.

challenging.for: He built and used telescopes, and made the most famous discoveries with them.
challenging.against: Telescopes were already being made and sold in the Netherlands in 1608, before Galileo built his first in 1609. He improved the design and was the first to use it with great skill on the sky.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake about who first made the telescope.

big_questions.q: Light slows down in glass and speeds up again when it comes out. Where does it get its speed back?
big_questions.hint: Light slows down because the tiny electrons in the glass pass it on. What happens when the light leaves the glass and there are no electrons to pass it on?

big_questions.q: A glass marble nearly vanishes in honey, but a diamond would not. Why not?
big_questions.hint: A diamond bends light much more than honey does. What happens at the edge of something that bends light differently?

big_questions.q: The light at the edge of a fish's round window came in at the lowest angle of all. What is that light doing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the biggest angle that light in water can have and still get out into the air.

big_questions.q: Each colour bends by a slightly different amount. What does that tell you about white light?
big_questions.hint: A prism and a raindrop both split white light. What must be hidden inside it?

big_questions.q: If you were a fish, would you say the sky is a small round window or a huge dome? Which is the truth?
big_questions.hint: Your eyes follow light straight back, but the light has been bent. Who is better placed to say, the fish or the diver?

big_questions.q: A mirage can be photographed. If a camera can see it, is it real or not?
big_questions.hint: The light is real. The place you think it came from is not.

big_questions.q: Spectacles were worn for more than 300 years before anyone could explain how they worked. Does something have to be explained before it can be useful?
big_questions.hint: Think of other things you use every day without knowing how they work.

big_questions.q: Whose job is it to make sure that every child who needs spectacles can get them?
big_questions.hint: Think of a child in a village far from an eye doctor, and what stands in the way: cost, distance, or not knowing.

story.title: The Round Window
story.note: The Gulf of Mannar, near Mandapam in Tamil Nadu, is a real place where women dive in shallow water for seaweed, which is dried and sold to make agar. Selvi, her grandmother Paati, her brother Murugan and everything that happens in the story are made up. The round window of sky and the silver ring seen from under the water are real, and they are seen best when the water is calm and clear.
text: Selvi was ten years old, and this was the morning her grandmother let her open her eyes under the sea.

They lived in a fishing village near Mandapam, on the Gulf of Mannar, where the women dive for seaweed. The seaweed is dried on the sand and sold, and far away it becomes the jelly in shops. Selvi's grandmother, Paati, had dived for it for fifty years.

They went out in a small boat at dawn, when the tide was low. Selvi's uncle rowed. Her little brother Murugan sat in the middle holding the anchor rope with both hands, because he was six and did not like the sea at all. The boat rocked on a patch of green water that was only three metres deep.

Paati tied a net bag round her waist and handed Selvi an old pair of swimming goggles, scratched but tight. 'Listen carefully,' she said. 'When you are on the bottom, look up. The sea will show you two faces.'
'Two faces?' said Selvi.

'In the middle there is a round window. Everything bright and clear is in the window, and the boat is in the middle of it. Around the window there is a silver ring. The silver ring is a mirror. Never swim toward the silver. Swim toward the window.' Then Paati slipped over the side, as easily as a fish, and was gone.
Selvi took a huge breath and followed her.

The sea was cool and green. Pale sunbeams hung in the water like ropes. Below her the sand was rippled like a plate of sevai, and brown seaweed grew in tufts between the stones. Paati was already there, bent over, filling her bag, her white hair floating about her head like smoke.
Selvi picked a handful of seaweed. Then she remembered, and looked up.

It was the strangest sight of her life. Straight above her was a round window, bright and sharp. In it was the whole sky, from one edge to the other, and the dark shape of the boat in the middle like a leaf. All around the window was a ring of shimmering silver. And in the silver, she could see the sea floor. She could see the sand, the stones and the brown tufts. She could even see Paati's feet. It was as if there was a second sea bed on the ceiling.

Her chest went tight. Which way was up? The floor was below her, and the floor was above her too. A wave rolled across the surface, and the silver ring rippled and tore like cloth. Selvi dropped the seaweed. A string of bubbles rushed out of her mouth. Her arms began to flap, and she did not know which way they should pull.

A hand closed on her wrist. It was Paati. She did not pull Selvi anywhere. She only pointed one finger, up, at the very middle of the round window. Then she pressed the palm of her other hand against the air in front of her, as if it were a mirror, and she shook her head.

Selvi understood. 'The silver is a mirror. It is only showing me the floor.' Her fear went quiet. She stopped looking at the silver. She fixed her eyes on the boat in the middle of the window, and kicked.

As she rose, the window shrank. It closed around her gently, smaller and smaller, as if the sea were pulling a drawstring. At last her head broke through the very middle of it, into the air and the noise and the sun.
'You were down there for ages!' shouted Murugan, leaning over the side. His face was green with worry. His uncle laughed and said it had been less than half a minute.

Paati came up beside her, breathing hard and smiling. In the boat she explained. 'Light from the sky bends when it goes down into the sea. All the sky, from one side to the other, gets squeezed into that one round window. But light from the sea floor, trying to come up at a low slant, cannot get out. The top of the sea sends it back down. At a low slant the top of the sea is a mirror. At a steep one it is a window. Two faces.'
'You told me,' said Selvi, 'and my head forgot.'
'Every head forgets once,' said Paati. 'The second time it remembers.'

That evening, while the seaweed lay drying on the sand like brown lace, Murugan stood at the edge of the water, with his arms folded and his feet far from the waves. Selvi filled a clear plastic tumbler from the kitchen and held it above his head. 'Look up through the side,' she said. 'Look at the top of the water.'

Murugan looked. The surface of the water in the tumbler shone like a silver plate, and in it he saw the bottom of the tumbler and his own finger. 'It is a mirror!' he said. Selvi tipped the tumbler a little. He moved his eye. 'Now it is a window!'
'Same water,' said Selvi. 'Same top. It only depends how the light comes at it.'
Murugan looked at the sea. Then, very slowly, he put one foot in.
story.epiphany: For the parent: light from the sky bends toward the normal as it goes down into the water, so the whole sky, from horizon to horizon, is squeezed into a cone about 97 degrees wide. That is the round window. At shallower angles, light going up from the sea bed meets the surface beyond the critical angle of about 49 degrees, and all of it is reflected. That is the silver ring, a mirror made by the water surface itself. The same surface is a window at one angle and a mirror at another. The window also shrinks as the diver rises, because its width depends on the depth.
ask: Why does the water's surface look like a mirror when you look up at it from a low slant, but like a window when you look straight up?
If the round window is made from the whole sky, what do you think is happening to the picture of the sky at the very edge of the window?
Why would the window of sky get smaller as a diver swims closer to the surface?
A diver looks up at the silver ring and sees the seabed there. Is the diver seeing a real place or a picture? What is the difference?
How could you check the two faces of the surface for yourself at home, without a sea?

how_we_found_out.story: Spectacles were first worn in Italy about 700 years ago. For more than 300 years, nobody could say why they helped. The old idea, taught since ancient Greece, was that the lens inside the eye is the part that sees, like a tiny screen. In 1604 the German astronomer Johannes Kepler worked out something different. The lens of the eye bends light to make a small upside-down picture on the back of the eye, the retina. If the eye bends light too much, the sharp picture forms in front of the retina, and the world looks blurry. A hollow lens in front of the eye can move the picture back. A bulging lens helps in the opposite case. A few years later Christoph Scheiner, a German astronomer, took the back coats from an ox eye. He looked through the thin back and saw the tiny upside-down picture glowing there. So the lens was not the screen. It only bends the light to make the picture.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: For centuries people believed that the lens inside the eye is the part that sees. Kepler showed that it bends light into a picture on the retina, and Scheiner showed that picture directly in an ox eye.

roots.context: We measured how light bends, and found the surface of water can be a window or a mirror. Now we ask what this tells us about things, about seeing, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Water Mirror activity, the underside of the water was a clear window when you looked up steeply, and a silver mirror when you looked at a slant. The water had not changed. Only the angle of the light had. So what a surface does depends on how the light meets it.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into windows and mirrors, as if each thing had one fixed nature. But a surface does one thing or the other depending on the angle of the light that meets it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Water Mirror activity, the underside of the water let you see through when you looked up steeply, and turned to a silver mirror when you looked at a slant. The box and the water did not change. Only the angle of your eye did. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: What you see depends on where you stand. A fish and a diver look at the same sky and see it differently.
three.what_is_life: Your own eyes bend light too. The lens inside your eye gets fatter for near things and thinner for far things. If the eyeball grows a little too long, the world goes blurry, and a spectacle lens fixes it.
three.what_is_this_world: One rule explains a pencil that looks snapped in water, a rainbow, a mirage, a sparkling diamond and a cable under the sea. The rule is that light changes speed when it crosses from one material into another.

roots.thread: One rule does all of this work. Light moves at different speeds in different materials, so it bends where they meet. At a steep angle it passes through the edge. At a shallow angle it is turned back. Nothing new is added for the rainbow, the diamond or the cable. The same light simply meets different edges at different angles. So these are not separate wonders. They are the same rule at work in different places.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the Buddhist story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: A king asks blind men to feel an elephant. One feels the head, one the tusk, one the leg, and each says what the elephant is like. They quarrel, because each is sure he is right. The Buddha says each has felt a part and taken it for the whole.
teachings.link: The surface of the water is a window to one eye and a mirror to another. Each is right about what they see, and wrong only if they say the surface can be nothing else.

teachings.teaching: The verse says that the face of truth is covered by a golden disc, and asks the Sun to uncover it so that the seeker can see.
teachings.link: A bright shining surface can hide as well as show. The silver ring shows the sea floor and hides the sky. You see more by moving to a new angle.

science.text: Total internal reflection is settled physics. It is the working principle of the optical fibres that carry most of the world's internet.

Physicists describe why light slows down in materials with different pictures, some in terms of waves adding up and some in terms of photons. They agree on the measured bends, but not always on the best picture.

other_view.view: A surface has fixed properties, such as its refractive index. Window and mirror are only two results of one rule, and the angle is just a number in that rule. Nothing here depends on who is looking.

practice.title: One glass, two faces
practice.say: Stand at a window at dusk. Switch on the room light and look at the glass. You see the room and your face. Now switch the room light off and wait. Look again. You see the world outside. Breathe in slowly three times. Ask yourself how one glass can show both.
practice.kid: Stand at a window at dusk with the light on. Look at the glass. Switch the light off. Look again. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: Is the surface of the water a window or a mirror, or is it neither until something looks at it?
A fish and a diver see the sky differently. Which one sees it as it really is?
The water's surface can be a window or a mirror, depending on the angle. What else might we have called one thing too quickly?
roots.art: A girl's eye looking up through a glass of water, with the surface shown half as a clear window to the ceiling and half as a silver mirror.

games.title: Toward, Away, Straight or Trapped?
games.players: 1 to 4 players. Alone, with a parent, or with friends.
games.context: This is a card game about the rule of the bend. For each card, players decide what the light does: bend toward the normal, bend away from it, go straight on, or get trapped.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a light journey on the front, and what the light does with the reason on the back

items.f: PRACTICE CARD. A torch beam goes at a slant from air into a tank of water.
items.b: TOWARD. Light slows down in water, so it bends toward the normal line.

items.f: A beam inside a tank of water reaches the surface at 20 degrees from the normal and goes out into the air.
items.b: AWAY. Light speeds up in air, so it bends away from the normal. At this small angle, it does get out.

items.f: A torch points straight down into a glass of water, along the normal.
items.b: STRAIGHT. Light that arrives along the normal does not bend.

items.f: A ray goes at a slant from air into a thick block of glass.
items.b: TOWARD. Glass slows light even more than water does, so the ray bends toward the normal.

items.f: A ray that went at a slant into a thick block of glass leaves it on the far side, back into the air.
items.b: AWAY. It bends away from the normal by the same amount, so it leaves parallel to the way it came in, but shifted sideways.

items.f: Light inside a diamond reaches the outside surface at 60 degrees from the normal.
items.b: TRAPPED. The critical angle of diamond is only about 24 degrees. At 60 degrees, all the light bounces back inside.

items.f: A diver on the sea bed looks up at the underside of the surface at a low slant, not straight above her.
items.b: TRAPPED. At a low slant, the surface is a mirror, and she sees the sea bed in it.

items.f: Light zigzags along a thin glass fibre in a cable under the sea.
items.b: TRAPPED. At each wall of the fibre the angle is shallow, so all the light is reflected back in.

items.f: Light in water reaches the surface at 60 degrees from the normal.
items.b: TRAPPED. The critical angle for water is about 49 degrees. At 60 degrees no light gets out.

items.f: Light in water reaches the surface at 30 degrees from the normal.
items.b: AWAY. 30 degrees is less than 49 degrees, so most of the light gets out, bending away from the normal.

items.f: Sunlight comes down from high, thin air into the thicker air near the ground.
items.b: TOWARD. Thicker air slows light very slightly, so the ray bends toward the normal, a tiny bit at a time.

items.f: Light from the sky goes down into the hot air just above a sun-baked road.
items.b: AWAY. Hot air is thinner and light moves a little faster in it. The ray bends away from the normal, bit by bit, and curves up to your eye. This makes a mirage.

items.f: A torch beam is shone into a jet of water pouring from a hole in a bottle.
items.b: TRAPPED. The light meets the edge of the curving jet at shallow angles, so it bounces back in and follows the jet.

items.f: A ray goes at a slant from air into cooking oil.
items.b: TOWARD. Oil slows light a little more than water does, so the ray bends toward the normal a little more.

items.f: A ray goes at a slant from water into glass.
items.b: TOWARD. Glass slows light more than water does, so the ray bends toward the normal, but only a little.

items.f: A ray goes at a slant from glass into water.
items.b: AWAY. The light speeds up a little, so it bends away from the normal a little.

items.f: A ray passes from honey into a glass marble sitting in the honey.
items.b: STRAIGHT, or nearly. Honey and glass slow light by almost the same amount, so there is hardly any bend, and the marble almost disappears.

items.f: A beam crosses a room full of still air.
items.b: STRAIGHT. In one material, where the speed is the same all through, light goes straight.

items.f: A ray goes from inside a glass block out into the air, along the normal.
items.b: STRAIGHT. Along the normal there is no bend, even though the light speeds up.

items.f: Light inside a glass prism in binoculars reaches a slanted face at 45 degrees from the normal.
items.b: TRAPPED. The critical angle of glass is about 42 degrees. At 45 degrees all the light bounces back, which is how binoculars turn the picture the right way up.

items.f: TEST IT. Sit on the floor next to a table. Stand a clear plastic box of water on a tray at the table's edge, above your eyes. Look up through the side at the top of the water, at a slant. What does the water's top do?
items.b: TRAPPED. At a slant, the top of the water turns silver, like a mirror. Light from below is bounced back down.

items.f: TEST IT. Stand a clear plastic box of water on a tray at the table's edge. Sit right under it and look straight up through the bottom and the top of the water. What do you see?
items.b: STRAIGHT. Looking straight up, the light comes along the normal, so it goes straight through. You see the ceiling. From here the top of the water is a window.

items.f: TEST IT. Stand a spoon in a glass of water and look at it from the side. The part under the water looks shifted. Which way does its light bend on the way to your eye?
items.b: AWAY. Light from the spoon speeds up when it leaves the water for the air, so it bends away from the normal. Your eyes follow it straight back, so the spoon looks shifted.

items.f: TEST IT. Put a clear glass marble in a bowl of honey, then in a bowl of water. In which bowl is it harder to see?
items.b: STRAIGHT, or nearly. In honey there is almost no bend where the marble meets the honey, so it is much harder to see than in water.

printables.title: Four playing mats
items: TOWARD: the light slows down, so it bends toward the normal line
AWAY: the light speeds up, so it bends away from the normal line
STRAIGHT: the light does not bend, or hardly bends at all
TRAPPED: the light bounces back and none of it gets out

printables.title: 20 normal-line tokens (small paper circles with a vertical line)

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 4 mats. Take the practice card out and put it to one side. Shuffle the other 23 cards and put them in a pile, face down. Put the tokens in a bowl.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front out loud. Do not show the back.
Decide what the light does. Put the card on the mat that fits. Is the light slowing down, speeding up, going along the normal, or arriving at a shallow angle inside a slow material?
Say why in one sentence, using the word slower, faster, normal or angle. If the other players agree it is a good reason, you win one token.
Then read the back out loud. If the mat was right, win one more token. A good reason with a wrong mat still wins the first token.
If you take a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together first. The first player to say what happened and why wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins. Players with equal tokens share the win. If you play alone, count your tokens and try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the four mats. Lay the mats on the floor. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. Fill a bowl with tokens. For the TEST IT cards, keep nearby a clear plastic box of water, a steel spoon and a glass marble. Add two small bowls, one of honey and one of water. Do not eat the test honey or water.
flow.say: Every card is a short journey of light. For each one, we decide. Does the light bend toward the normal, bend away, go straight, or get trapped?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mats. Lay out the four mats. Shuffle the cards. Put them face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the card game Toward, Away, Straight or Trapped. You set it up.
flow.parent: The normal is the imaginary upright line standing out from a surface. If your child has not met it yet, draw it on the floor mat with chalk or tape, and explain it in one sentence. With 2 to 4 players, take turns as reader and judge. The player on the left reads the back.

flow.do: Take the practice card. Read the front out loud. Ask your child to guess the mat and give a reason. Then read the back. Put the card on its mat. Nobody wins a token.
flow.say: Let's practise. A torch beam goes at a slant from air into water. Which mat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Practice card. A beam goes at a slant from air into water. Which mat?

check.q: A torch beam goes at a slant from air into a tank of water. What does the light do?
check.why: Light moves more slowly in water than in air, so it bends toward the normal. Choosing away means mixing up the two directions. Away is for light leaving water. Choosing straight means forgetting that the beam comes in at a slant.

flow.context: In this step, you play the practice card together, to learn how the game works.

flow.do: Take turns. Each player takes the top card, reads the front, puts it on a mat and gives a reason. Then they read the back. Give tokens as the rules say.
flow.say: Read your card. Tell us which mat, and why, in one sentence. Then read the back and see.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a card. Pick a mat. Say why. Check the back.
flow.parent: A good reason uses the words slower, faster, normal or angle. Give the first token for a good reason even when the mat is wrong. The diamond, diver, fibre, 60-degree water, water jet and binocular prism cards all go on TRAPPED. The straight-down torch, honey marble, still air and along-the-normal cards go on STRAIGHT. The mirage card is AWAY, because the light moves faster in the hot air. Each card has its answer on the back.

ask.q: What do the cards on the TRAPPED mat have in common?
good: The light is inside a slow material, like water, glass or a diamond.
The light reaches the edge at a shallow angle.
The light would have to bend away so much that it cannot leave.

flow.context: In this step, you play the main part of the game, taking turns with the cards.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop the game and do the test together. Everyone guesses first. Then try it and read the back.
flow.say: A TEST IT card. Before we try it, everyone say what you think will happen and why. Then we look.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card. First guess what will happen. Why do you think so? Then try it.

ask.q: The same top of the water was a mirror in one test and a window in another. What changed?
good: The angle you looked from.
The slant of the light reaching the top of the water.
Nothing about the water changed, only the angle.

flow.think: The water did not change between the two tests. So what makes a surface a mirror or a window?
flow.context: In this step, you try one of the TEST IT cards together.

flow.do: Count the tokens to find the winner. Then look at the TRAPPED mat together and read its cards again.
flow.say: Let's count the tokens. Then look at the TRAPPED mat. Where do we use trapped light in real life?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Look at the TRAPPED mat. Where is trapped light used?
flow.think: Trapped light can travel round a bend. What could you send along it?
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and think about where trapped light is used.

setup.caption: 3. For TEST IT cards, everyone tries the test.

experiments.title: Measure the Bend: how much does water turn a beam?
experiments.question: A thin beam of torch light goes from air into water at a slant. Does the water turn the beam toward the normal or away from it? By how much? And does the turn get bigger when the slant gets bigger?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When the beam goes in at 60 degrees from the normal, will it turn toward the normal or away from it, and by about how many degrees? What will it do when it goes in straight on? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The box, the water, the torch, the slit card and the spot where the beam goes in stay the same every time. Only the angle of the torch changes. You measure every angle twice, with the same protractor, because one try can be a fluke. You read each angle from the normal line, not from the surface.
results_table: Angle of the torch beam in the air (degrees from the normal)
Angle in the water, first try (degrees)
Angle in the water, second try (degrees)
How many degrees did the water turn the beam?
Did it turn toward or away from the normal?

materials.item: a clear rectangular plastic food box with flat, straight sides, about 15 centimetres long, 10 centimetres wide and 6 centimetres deep (choose one with square corners, not rounded ones)
about 450 millilitres of water, which is a depth of 3 centimetres in the box, and optionally 3 drops of milk to make the beam show in the water

a small LED torch (a pen torch or key-ring torch lies flat best; a phone torch also works if you prop the phone on its long edge with clay so its light faces sideways), with a piece of black card or thick black paper about 8 centimetres by 5 centimetres taped over its front. A grown-up cuts one thin vertical slit in the card, 2 millimetres wide and 3 centimetres tall
a big sheet of plain white paper, such as A3 chart paper, a pencil, a ruler and a protractor
masking tape to hold the sheet down, and a few coins to keep the box from sliding
a room that can be made dark, such as a room with curtains closed in the evening, and a cloth to wipe up spills

experiments.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes. A grown-up cuts the slit, and uses scissors or a craft knife on a firm table. Keep the phone away from the water, and wipe up spills at once, because a wet floor is slippery. Do not drink the water, especially if you added milk. If anyone at home is allergic to milk, leave it out.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the bend diagram for your 60 degree try: the surface line, the normal, the beam in the air in one colour and the beam in the water in another, with both angles written on it. Last, write what you think, what you saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: angle of the beam in the water for four angles in the air
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will differ by a few degrees. Your own bars should be shorter than the angle in the air, and should grow as it grows.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you shine a thin beam of light into water at four different slants and measure how much the water turns it. You use a protractor, a plastic box of water and a torch with a slit.

setup.art: A big sheet of white paper with a straight line near the middle, an upright dotted line through its centre marked O, and three lines fanning out from O marked 20, 40 and 60 degrees, with a protractor on one of them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the surface line, the normal at O, and lines at 20, 40 and 60 degrees.

setup.art: A clear plastic box of water with its long front wall exactly on the surface line and its left end a little to the left of O, with a few coins holding it still.
setup.caption: 2. Put the box of water on the sheet, with its front wall on the surface line.

setup.art: A phone torch lying flat on the paper with a black card taped over it, a thin vertical slit in the card, sending a bright thin line along the 40 degree line toward O.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the torch with its slit at the end of one line, aimed at O.

setup.art: A top view of the box: a bright line coming in at the left, bending toward the normal in the milky water, and leaving at the far wall as a bright line on the paper, with two pencil dots on it.
setup.caption: 4. In the dark, mark two dots on the bright line that comes out of the far wall.

setup.art: The same sheet with a pencil line drawn from O to the point where the outgoing line meets the far wall, and a protractor measuring the angle from the normal.
setup.caption: 5. Join O to that point. Measure the angle from the normal with the protractor.

flow.do: Show your child the box, the water and the torch. Ask for a guess about the 60 degree beam and the reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will shine a thin beam into water at a slant. Will the water turn the beam toward the upright line, or away from it? By how much? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A beam goes into water at a slant. Which way does it turn? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think will happen when the beam goes in straight on?
good: It will go straight through.
It will not bend, because it is not at a slant.
It will bend a lot, because the water is in the way.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write down the guess and the reason. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch, one marks the dots, one measures with the protractor and one writes; swap roles for each angle. Each child can draw their own bend diagram. Nobody needs more than one box. Remind your child that the normal is the upright line standing at right angles to the surface.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Measure the Bend experiment. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Tape the big sheet of paper down. 2. Draw a straight line 15 centimetres long across the middle. Call its middle point O. 3. Use the protractor to draw a line through O at a right angle to the first line. This is the normal. 4. On the upper side, draw lines from O at 20, 40 and 60 degrees from the normal, each 15 centimetres long. Label each line.
flow.say: First we draw the map. This line is the surface of the water. The upright line through O is the normal. The three slanted lines show where the torch will stand.
flow.kid: Draw a 15 centimetre line. Mark its middle O. Draw the normal. Add lines at 20, 40 and 60 degrees.
flow.parent: Draw the upright line first. A right angle is 90 degrees on the protractor. Set the protractor's middle hole on O. The slanted lines must be measured from the normal, not from the surface line. Put O a little to the right of the middle of the sheet, so that the 60 degree line fits on the paper.

check.q: In this test, where do you measure the angles from?
options: From the normal line, standing at a right angle to the surface
From the flat surface of the water
From the edge of the paper
check.why: Scientists always measure the bend of light from the normal. A beam coming in along the normal has an angle of 0 degrees and does not bend. Measuring from the surface instead would give the wrong numbers, such as 90 degrees for a beam that goes straight in.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the map on the paper that you will use for the whole test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a thin vertical slit, 2 millimetres wide and 3 centimetres tall, in the black card. Tape the card over the front of the torch. Lay the torch on its side (or prop the phone on its long edge), so the slit stands upright and touches the paper. Check in the dark that a thin bright line shows on the paper.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts the slit. The slit makes the light into a thin standing sheet. Where the sheet touches the paper, it draws a thin bright line.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a thin slit in black card. Tape it over the torch.
flow.parent: The slit must stand upright when the torch lies on its side, and its bottom must touch the paper. If the line is too faint, make the slit 3 millimetres wide, or use a brighter torch. If it is too wide and fuzzy, use a narrower slit. Phone torches work only in a really dark room, and the line is fainter, so a small LED torch is better. If you see only a glow and no line, make the slit a little wider (3 millimetres) and put the torch closer to the box.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the slit card, so that the torch gives a thin bright line to measure.

flow.do: Put the box on the paper. Its long front wall goes on the surface line. Its left end goes about 4 centimetres left of O. Pour in the water, 3 centimetres deep. Add the milk, if you use it. Switch off the room light. Lay the torch at the end of the normal line, pointing at O. Look at where the bright line leaves the far wall.
flow.say: First the straight-on beam. The torch is on the normal line. Watch the line that comes out of the far wall. Does it carry on straight, or does it bend?
flow.kid: Put the torch on the normal line. Switch off the light. Does the beam bend?

ask.q: Did the beam bend when it went in straight on? What does that tell you?
good: No, it carried on straight.
Light that arrives along the normal does not bend.
The bend only happens when the beam is slanted.

check.q: The torch shines straight along the normal into the water. What does the beam do?
check.why: Light that arrives along the normal meets the water straight on, so no part of it reaches the water before another. It does not turn. Choosing bends toward the normal usually means thinking the water always bends light, even straight on. The bend only happens when light arrives at a slant.

flow.parent: The outgoing line should lie exactly on the normal line. If it is off to one side, the box is crooked. Straighten it, and try again. Expect the straight-on beam to be slightly dimmer than the slanted ones. That is normal.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the box and the torch, and test the beam that goes in straight on.

flow.do: Move the torch to the end of the 20 degree line, aimed at O. In the dark, find the bright line that comes out of the far wall. Mark two dots on it with a pencil, one near the wall and one 8 centimetres away. Draw a line through the dots back to the wall. Call the point where it meets the wall E. Draw a line from O to E. Measure the angle between the line OE and the normal. Write it down. Do the same for 40 and 60 degrees. Then do all three again.
flow.say: Now the slanted beams. Mark two dots on the bright line that comes out. Draw back to the wall. Join that point to O. That is the path of the light inside the water. Measure its angle from the normal.
flow.kid: Put the torch on the 20 degree line. Mark two dots on the bright line. Join them to O.
flow.parent: Why this works. The beam comes out of the far wall parallel to the way it went in, so the bright line outside points straight back to the spot E where it left the water. The path in the water is the line from O to E. Typical results are about 15 degrees for 20, about 29 for 40 and about 41 for 60. Your numbers may be 3 to 5 degrees off, because the beam is not perfectly thin. That is fine. If the beam in the water is faint, take out the milk, or add one more drop. If the outgoing line is too faint to mark, put the two dots at its brightest part, or make the room darker and try again. If your angles are all bigger than the angle in the air, check that you measured from the normal.
flow.context: In this step, you measure how far the water turns the beam for three different slants, twice each.

flow.do: Fill in the table. For each angle, work out the average of the two tries. Then take the average angle in the water away from the angle in the air. This is how many degrees the water turned the beam. Write toward or away.
flow.say: Fill in the table. For 60 degrees in the air, how many degrees did you measure in the water? So by how many degrees did the water turn the beam? Toward the normal or away?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Work out how many degrees the water turned the beam.

check.q: As the angle in the air got bigger, what happened to the angle in the water?
options: It got bigger too, but it always stayed smaller than the angle in the air
It got bigger than the angle in the air
check.why: The water turns the beam toward the normal, so the angle in the water is always smaller than the angle in the air. A bigger slant gives a bigger turn. Choosing that it stayed the same usually means only looking at one angle. Choosing bigger than the air angle means mixing up the direction of the bend.

flow.context: In this step, you put your measurements in a table and work out how much the water turned the beam each time.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Compare with the guess from the start. Write the answer under the diagram.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think at the start? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What do you think now, what did you see, and why did it happen?
good: The water bent the beam toward the normal. At 60 degrees in the air I measured about 40 degrees in the water. Light slows down in water, so it turns.
The bigger the slant, the bigger the turn. At 0 degrees there was no turn.
The angle in the water was always smaller than the angle in the air.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses their own numbers, says toward the normal, and mentions that light moves more slowly in water. If their numbers are different from the expected ones, do not worry. Ask what could make the beam hard to measure, such as a wide beam or a crooked box.
flow.think: If the beam went from the water back into the air, which way would it turn?
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist: what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Build an Eye That Needs Spectacles
experiments.question: A magnifying glass can make a sharp picture of a faraway window on a card, just as the lens in an eye makes a picture on the retina. What happens when the card is a little too far back, as in a short-sighted eye, or too near, as in a long-sighted eye? Can a spectacle lens fix it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you move the card back a little, will the picture stay sharp? Will a lens from a short-sighted person's spectacles fix it, or a lens from reading spectacles? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The magnifying glass, the window and the room stay the same. You never change the magnifying glass in your model eye. Only the place of the card and the spectacle lens in front change. Each time, you slide the card slowly to find the sharpest picture, and you check it twice.
results_table: Distance from the magnifying glass to the card for the sharpest picture (centimetres)
Was the picture of the window sharp, blurry or too dim to tell?

materials.item: a hand magnifying glass, about 8 to 10 centimetres across
a white card or a sheet of paper stuck on thin cardboard, about 15 centimetres square, to be the retina
a long ruler or a measuring tape, modelling clay or a stack of books to hold the magnifying glass upright, and a second stack for the card
a bright window, or a bright lamp in a dark room, at least 3 metres from the magnifying glass (point at the bright sky or a lit window, never at the Sun)

a pair of spectacles worn by someone who is short-sighted (any strength from about minus 1.5 upward works; a stronger pair gives a clearer result). Check them: print looks smaller through the lens, so it is a hollow lens
