a pair of reading spectacles. Check them: print looks bigger through the lens, so it is a bulging lens

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun through the magnifying glass or the spectacle lenses, and never leave them where sunlight shines through them onto paper, cloth or skin, because they can start a fire or burn. Borrowed spectacles belong to someone, so hold them by the frame and give them back unscratched.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw your model eye from the side: the magnifying glass, the card and the window, with the light from the window bending in the lens to a point on the card. Draw it once for the sharp picture and once for the blurry picture. Last, write what you think, what you saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you use a magnifying glass and a white card as a model of an eye. You move the card to make the model short-sighted or long-sighted, and then you use spectacle lenses to fix it.

setup.art: A magnifying glass standing upright in clay on a table, a white card behind it on a stack of books, and a bright window far away, with a ruler along the table.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the magnifying glass upright. Put the card behind it. Face a bright window.

setup.art: A small, sharp upside-down picture of a bright window glowing on the white card, with a hand sliding the card along a ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Slide the card until the picture of the window is sharp. Measure the distance.

setup.art: The same picture, now blurry, with the card moved a little back, and a pair of short-sighted spectacles held in front of the magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 3. Move the card back. The picture goes blurry. Hold a hollow lens in front.

setup.art: The card moved closer than the sharp place, a blurry picture, and a pair of reading spectacles held in front of the magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 4. Move the card closer. The picture goes blurry. Hold a bulging lens in front.

flow.do: Show your child the magnifying glass, the card and the two pairs of spectacles. Check which pair makes print look smaller. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: A magnifying glass can make a small picture of a window on a card. That is a little like your eye. If we move the card back, what will happen to the picture? Can a spectacle lens fix it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A lens can make a picture of a window. What if the card is too far back? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think moving the card might change the picture?
good: The light comes together at one place only.
The picture is only sharp at the right distance.
It will stay the same, because the lens is the same.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, one holds the magnifying glass steady in clay, one slides the card, one reads the ruler and one writes; swap for each step. Do not correct the guess. Let your child test each pair of spectacles by looking at print through the lens. The pair where print looks smaller has hollow lenses, which are for short sight. The pair where print looks bigger has bulging lenses.
flow.context: This is the first step of the model eye experiment. You look at two pairs of spectacles and guess before you test.

flow.do: Stand the magnifying glass upright in clay, facing the window. Hold the card behind it and slide the card slowly toward and away from the lens. Stop where the picture of the window is sharpest. Measure the distance from the lens to the card in centimetres. Write it down. Check it a second time.
flow.say: Slide the card slowly. At one distance, a small, sharp picture of the window appears. It will be upside down. When it looks sharpest, measure the distance and write it down.
flow.kid: Slide the card back and forth. Find where the window looks sharp. Measure the distance.
flow.parent: Switch off the room light, if the window is not very bright, or stand in a shaded part of the room. The picture is upside down, as in a real eye. The sharp distance is the focal length of your magnifying glass. It is usually between 10 and 30 centimetres. Mark the place on the ruler, because you will want to come back to it.

check.q: The picture of the window on the card is sharp at one distance only. What does that tell you about a lens?
options: A lens brings light together to a sharp point at one distance behind it
A lens works only in the dark
A lens makes pictures at any distance
check.why: A bulging lens bends all the light from a faraway thing to meet at one spot. In front of or behind that spot, the light is spread out, so the picture is blurry. This is why an eye must be exactly the right length, or have the right lens.

flow.context: In this step, you find the sharp place for the picture of the window and measure its distance.

flow.do: Move the card 3 centimetres further back. The picture goes blurry. This is your short-sighted eye. Now hold the hollow spectacle lens right in front of the magnifying glass, touching it. Slide the card to find the new sharp place. Measure the distance. Write down what happened.
flow.say: Move the card back by a few centimetres. The picture goes blurry. This is like an eyeball that is a little too long. Now put the short-sighted spectacle lens in front. Slide the card again. What do you find?
flow.kid: Move the card back 3 centimetres. It is blurry. Hold the hollow lens in front. Slide the card.

ask.q: Where did the sharp picture move to when you added the hollow lens?
good: It moved further back, away from the magnifying glass.
The card had to be further back to get a sharp picture.
The hollow lens made the light come together later.

check.q: The hollow lens moved the sharp picture further back. Which eye problem does this fix?
options: Short sight, where the picture forms in front of the retina
Long sight, where the picture forms behind the retina
check.why: In a short-sighted eye, the picture forms too early, in front of the retina. A hollow lens spreads the light a little first, so the picture forms further back, on the retina. Choosing long sight mixes up the two problems. Long sight needs the opposite fix.

flow.parent: Typically the sharp place moves back by about 3 to 6 centimetres, but it depends on the strength of the two lenses, so your number will differ. A spectacle lens is smaller than the magnifying glass, so the picture will be dimmer; hold the lens flat against the middle of the magnifying glass and dim the room. If the picture never gets sharp, the lens is weak, or the card is not far enough back. Try moving the card back 6 centimetres. If nobody at home is short-sighted, skip this step and ask your child to draw what they think would happen.
flow.context: In this step, you make the model eye short-sighted by moving the card back. Then you fix it with a hollow lens, as spectacles do.

flow.do: Put the card back at the sharp place. Then move it 2 centimetres closer to the lens. The picture goes blurry. This is your long-sighted eye. Hold the reading spectacle lens right in front of the magnifying glass, touching it. Slide the card to find the new sharp place. Measure the distance. Write down what happened.
flow.say: Now move the card closer. The picture goes blurry. This is like an eyeball that is a little too short. Put the reading spectacle lens in front. Slide the card again. What do you find?
flow.kid: Move the card 2 centimetres closer. It is blurry. Hold the reading lens in front. Slide the card.

ask.q: Where did the sharp picture move to when you added the bulging lens?
good: It moved closer to the magnifying glass.
The card had to be nearer to get a sharp picture.
The bulging lens made the light come together sooner.

flow.parent: Typically the sharp place moves closer by about 2 to 4 centimetres, depending on the strength. Record how far it moved in centimetres, and compare it with the hollow lens: which moved it more? If the move is too small to see, try a stronger pair, or two pairs held together.
flow.context: In this step, you make the model eye long-sighted by moving the card closer. Then you fix it with a bulging lens, as reading spectacles do.

flow.do: Fill in the table with your three sharp distances. Draw the model eye for the sharp picture and the blurry picture. Compare your results with the guess from the start.
flow.say: Look at your table. For the plain model eye, where was the sharp place? With the hollow lens, did it move back or forward? With the reading lens?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Draw the model eye. Was your guess right?
flow.parent: A good table has three distances in centimetres. The hollow lens moves the sharp place back. The bulging lens moves it closer.
flow.context: In this step, you write down your results and draw your model eye.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Write the answer under the drawing.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think at the start? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What do you think now, what did you see, and why did it happen?
good: A spectacle lens can move the sharp place of the picture. My hollow lens moved it back by about 5 centimetres. Hollow lenses spread the light, so it comes together later.
The picture is only sharp at one distance, so an eye that is too long or too short needs a lens to fix it.
The reading lens moved the sharp picture closer, because bulging lenses bend light more.

flow.think: Spectacles move the sharp picture to where the back of the eye is. Why can they not shorten or lengthen the eye itself?
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist: what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: The Water Mirror: when the window turns silver

materials.item: a clear plastic box with flat sides (a food box or a see-through container), or a clear plastic jar
water to fill it three quarters full
a tray or a large basin for the box to stand in, a towel, and a table or a stool with a stack of books so that the box sits above your eyes when you sit on the floor
a pencil or a coin

schedule.what: Guess. Look up at the water from below at a slant and from straight below. Find where the window turns into a mirror. Explain it.

activities.record: A drawing of the box from the side, with the eye in two places. Mark the place where the underside of the water looked clear, and the place where it looked silver. Write one sentence on what changed.
activities.safety: Keep the box in a tray and never hold it above anyone's head. Have a towel ready. A wet floor is slippery, so wipe up spills at once.
activities.context: In this activity, you sit on the floor and look up at the underside of the water in a clear box on a table. You find the place where the water's top turns from a window into a mirror.

setup.art: A child sitting on the floor beside a table, looking up through the side of a clear box of water in a tray above eye level, at a steep angle and seeing the ceiling light.
setup.caption: 1. Put the box of water above your eyes. Look up steeply.

setup.art: The same child looking up at a much lower slant, and the underside of the water shining silver with a pencil tip reflected in it.
setup.caption: 2. Look at a low slant. The underside of the water turns silver.

setup.art: A side drawing of the water box with two eye positions and two sight lines to the water's top, one passing through and one bouncing back.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the two sight lines. One goes through. One bounces.

flow.do: Show your child the box of water. Ask what the top of the water will look like if you look up at it from underneath. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: The box of water will be above our eyes, and we will look up at the top of the water from underneath. What do you think we will see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look up at the top of water from underneath. What will you see? Why?

ask.q: Do you think you will see through the top of the water to the ceiling?
good: Yes, because water is see-through.
Maybe, but not from every angle.
No, because the top of the water will be a mirror.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. With 2 to 4 children, take turns to look; one child at a time sits on the floor by the box while the others wait with the towel.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Mirror. You guess before you look.

flow.do: Stand the box in the tray at the edge of a table or on books. Its bottom must be above your eyes when you sit on the floor beside it. Sit close and look up through the side wall at the underside of the water, at a low slant. A grown-up pushes a pencil tip under the surface from above, so you can see it and its reflection.
flow.say: The box is above your eyes. Look up through the side, at a low slant, at the top of the water. What do you see? What happens to the pencil tip?
flow.kid: The box is above your eyes. Look up through the side. What does the top of the water look like?
flow.parent: A flat-sided box shows the effect more clearly than a round glass, because round glass bends the view. The underside of the water should look like a bright silver sheet, and the pencil tip may show up twice, once itself and once reflected. Never carry or hold a full box above a child's head. If you see nothing special, look at a lower slant, with your eyes level with the bottom of the box.

check.q: At a low slant, the underside of the water looked silver, like a mirror. What was it doing with the light?
options: Bouncing all the light from below back down into the water
check.why: At a low slant, light going up through the water meets the top at an angle bigger than the critical angle, about 49 degrees from the normal. None of it can get out, so all of it bounces back down. That is total internal reflection. The surface lets light through only when you look up steeply.

flow.context: In this step, you look up at the underside of the water at a low slant, and see the silver mirror.

flow.do: Now raise your eyes slowly, so you look more and more steeply up at the water. Notice the place where the silver sheet gives way to a clear window, and you see the ceiling. Move your head up and down a few times to find the place. A helper marks on the box, with a sticky note, where your eye was when the silver turned clear. Then pour out half the water and test again. Does the silver turn clear at the same angle? Last, look straight up through the bottom of the box, if it is clear.
flow.say: Raise your eyes slowly. Where does the silver stop? What can you see in the clear part? Can you find the place where it changes?
flow.kid: Look more steeply. Find where the silver turns clear. What do you see then?
flow.parent: The change happens roughly where your line of sight makes an angle of about 40 degrees with the water's top, which is about 50 degrees from the normal. Your child may find that it is hard to find the exact place. That is fine. It is the idea that matters. The flip angle is the same with half the water, because it depends on the angle, not on how much water there is. If nothing silver shows, sit closer to the box, and use a box with clean, dry, scratch-free walls.
flow.think: The water did not change. Only your angle of looking did. So what decides whether the top of the water is a window or a mirror?
flow.context: In this step, you find where the silver mirror turns back into a clear window.

flow.do: Draw the box from the side, with the eye in two places. For each place, draw the line of sight to the underside of the water. Draw one going through, and one bouncing back. Write one sentence on what changed.
flow.say: Draw the box from the side. Draw two sight lines to the top of the water. One goes through, and one bounces. Write one sentence about what changed.
flow.kid: Draw the box. Draw two sight lines. One goes through. One bounces.

ask.q: Why is the top of the water a window from one place and a mirror from another?
good: At a steep angle the light passes through. At a shallow angle it cannot get out, so it bounces back.
The angle of the light changes what the surface does.
Beyond about 49 degrees from the normal, all the light is bounced back.

flow.context: In this step, you draw your two sight lines and write what changed.

activities.title: Shimmer Watch: the road that looks wet

materials.item: a window, terrace or balcony with a view along a road or a dark paved path on a hot, sunny day
a phone with a camera that can zoom
a dosa tawa or flat steel pan, heated by an adult and left on the stove (or a hair dryer on its hot setting, if you prefer no hot pan)
a sheet of paper with thick black stripes drawn across it with a marker, about 8 stripes

schedule.what: Look along a hot road for a shiny patch. Then, with a grown-up, watch stripes wobble above a hot plate. Explain what you saw.

activities.record: A drawing of the shiny patch on the road, with the sky in it. A drawing of the wobbling stripes. A sentence on why light bends in hot air.
activities.safety: A grown-up heats the plate and the plate stays where it is, on the stove with the flame or ring switched off. It stays hot for many minutes and can burn badly. Do not touch it, and keep children an arm's length away. Do not use any plastic near it. Stay at the window or terrace for the road part, never on the road.
activities.context: In this activity, you look for the shiny patch that appears on a hot road, and you look through the air above a hot plate to see light bending in hot air.

setup.art: A child at a window on a hot afternoon, looking along a straight road where a shiny wet-looking patch shines in the distance and a lorry is mirrored upside down in it.
setup.caption: 1. Look along a hot road for a shiny patch.

setup.art: A steel tawa on a heat-proof mat at the edge of a table, with a striped paper standing 30 centimetres behind it and a child crouching with her eye level with the plate.
setup.caption: 2. With a grown-up, look across a hot plate at the stripes.

setup.art: A close view of wavy stripes seen above a hot plate, with rising heat shown as curly lines.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the stripes as they wobble.

flow.do: On a hot sunny afternoon, stand at a window or on a terrace. You need a view along a road or a dark paved path. Look at the far part of the road. Look for a shiny patch that looks like water. Zoom in with the phone, and take a picture. Compare it with the same road in the evening, if you can.
flow.say: Look along the road, far into the distance. Do you see a shiny patch that looks like water? Zoom in with the phone and take a picture. What do you think it is?
flow.kid: Look far along a hot road. Do you see a shiny patch? Take a picture.
flow.parent: A mirage needs a hot, sunny day and a long, flat, dark surface seen from a low angle. It may not appear if it is cloudy, or if you are looking at a short road. If you see nothing, do the hot plate in the next step. The shiny patch is a picture of the sky. In the zoomed picture, look for upside-down cars or poles.

ask.q: Does the shiny patch get closer as you look? Does it feel like real water?
good: No, it stays far away.
It looks like water but is probably the sky.
I do not know. It looks wet, but cars are not splashing.

flow.context: In this step, you look for a mirage on a hot road, and photograph it.

flow.do: First look across the cold plate at the striped paper, 30 centimetres behind it, with your eyes level with the plate. The stripes stay still. Then a grown-up heats the plate for 2 minutes and switches off the stove, without moving the plate. Look again from an arm's length away. Watch for 1 minute, and count how many stripes wobble. (With a hair dryer, a grown-up blows hot air across the line of sight instead.)
flow.say: A grown-up will heat the plate and leave it on the stove. Do not touch it. Crouch down and look across the top of the plate at the stripes. What do the stripes do?
flow.kid: Look at the stripes over the cold plate. A grown-up heats it. Do not touch it. Look again.
flow.parent: Keep children at arm's length from the plate. The stripes should wave and wobble within a few seconds, as the hot air rises. The cold plate is your fair-test comparison. The plate stays hot for 10 minutes or more. When you finish, leave it on the stove until cool and keep children away. With 2 to 4 children, take turns to look while one holds the striped paper, and everyone draws. If the wobble is faint, use a hotter plate (3 minutes), thicker stripes, or look in a dim kitchen with a bright window behind the stripes.

check.q: The stripes wobbled when you looked through the air above the hot plate. What bent the light?
options: Hot air rising from the plate, which bends light differently from cool air
check.why: Hot air is thinner than cool air, so light moves a little faster in it, and it bends. The hot air rises in moving streams, so the bending keeps changing, and the stripes wobble. Choosing the plate itself is a common idea, but the plate is not see-through. It is the air above it that bends the light.

flow.context: In this step, with a grown-up, you look across the top of a hot plate and see light bending in hot air.

flow.do: Draw the stripes as you saw them above the hot plate. Draw the road mirage if you saw one. Write one sentence on why the stripes wobbled, and one on why the road looked wet.
flow.say: Draw what you saw. The wobbling stripes, and the shiny road, if you saw it. Then write a sentence on why light bends in hot air.
flow.kid: Draw the wobbling stripes. Write why they wobbled.

ask.q: Why does the road look wet when it is dry?
good: Light from the sky bends in the hot air above the road, and curves up to your eyes. You see a picture of the sky on the road.
It is a picture of the sky made by bent light.
Hot air near the ground bends the light, so the sky looks like it is on the road.

flow.context: In this step, you draw what you saw and explain why light bends in hot air.

activities.title: The Glowing Water Jet

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with smooth, straight sides, 1 or 2 litres, with its label peeled off and its cap on
a bright LED torch (a phone torch works only in a very dark room), and sticky tape to hold it
a nail for a grown-up to make one small hole (a thick needle also works), about 3 millimetres wide, 4 centimetres from the bottom of the bottle
a kitchen sink, or a big tray or basin to catch the water, and a towel
a room that can be made dark, and a jug of water to top up the bottle

schedule.what: Guess. Make a hole in a bottle. Fill it with water, shine a torch in from the far side, and watch the jet glow. Explain it.

activities.record: A drawing of the bottle, the torch and the curved jet, with the light shown following the jet. One sentence on why the light stays inside the water.
activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole (a sharp point), holding the bottle firmly against a table and pushing the nail slowly away from their hand; children stay back until it is done. Do the pouring over the sink or the tray, and keep the phone or torch away from the water. Wipe up spills, because wet floors are slippery.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a jet of water pour from a bottle in a dark room and shine a torch along it. You find that the light follows the jet round its curve.

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a nail through the side of a plastic bottle, near the bottom, while a child holds a towel.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes one small hole near the bottom.

setup.art: A bottle full of water with a thumb over the hole, a torch taped to the opposite side aimed at the hole, standing at the edge of a sink.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle. Tape the torch opposite the hole, aimed at it.

setup.art: A dark room: a glowing curved jet of water arcing from the bottle into the sink, bright all along its length, with a bright splash where it lands.
setup.caption: 3. In the dark, take away your thumb. The jet glows.

flow.do: Show your child the bottle and the torch. Ask what the light will do when the torch shines into the water and a jet of water pours out of the bottle. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will shine a torch through a bottle of water, toward a hole, and let the water pour out in a jet. Will the light go straight on, past the jet, or follow the water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Shine a torch at a water jet. Will the light follow the water? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the light might go straight, or follow the curve?
good: Light goes in straight lines, so it should go straight.
The water is see-through, so the light goes through.
Maybe the light is trapped in the water.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch, one holds the bottle, one watches the splash and one draws. Make a bottle each if you have spare bottles, or take turns. Do not correct the guess. Light going straight is the usual first idea, and it is a good one to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glowing Water Jet. You guess before you try.

flow.do: A grown-up uses the nail to make one small hole, about 3 millimetres wide, in the side of the bottle, 4 centimetres from the bottom. Cover the hole with a small piece of tape. Fill the bottle with water. Put the cap on.
flow.say: A grown-up makes the hole. We cover it with tape for now. Then we fill the bottle with water. Keep it over the sink.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a small hole. Cover it with tape. Fill the bottle with water.
flow.parent: Make the hole as clean and round as you can, because a rough hole makes a ragged jet. Hold the bottle against the table, and push the nail slowly. If the hole is bigger than 4 millimetres, the jet will be too wild. Work over the sink.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the hole and the bottle is filled.

flow.do: Stand the bottle at the edge of the sink, with the hole facing into the sink. Tape the torch to the side of the bottle opposite the hole, aimed at the hole. Switch off the room light. Take off the cap and the tape. Watch the jet. Hold your finger in the jet near the sink and look at the splash. Then tilt the torch so it no longer points at the hole, and see whether the jet still glows. Top up the bottle with the jug, because the jet gets weaker as the water falls.
flow.say: Switch the torch on, and the room light off. Take off the tape and the cap. What does the jet look like? What does the splash look like?
flow.kid: Aim the torch at the hole. Switch the room light off. Take the tape off. Watch.

ask.q: Does the light go straight on, or follow the curve of the water?
good: It follows the curve, and the jet glows all along.
The light stays inside the water.
The jet glows and the splash lights up where the light finally escapes.

check.q: The jet glowed all the way along its curve. What was keeping the light inside the water?
options: Total internal reflection, with the light bouncing off the edge of the jet
check.why: Light inside the jet meets the edge of the water at a shallow angle each time, beyond the critical angle of about 49 degrees. So all of it bounces back in. It zigzags along the curve of the jet. Gravity pulls the water into its curve, but it does not hold the light in the jet.

flow.parent: If the jet does not glow, make the room darker, bring the torch closer to the hole, and make sure it is aimed right at the hole. A thinner, steadier jet works best. A bright LED torch works better than a phone torch. Fill the bottle again, and try once more. Typical result: a glowing jet for the first 10 seconds or so, which fades as the bottle empties. The torch tilted away gives a much dimmer jet, so the aim is part of the proof.
flow.context: In this step, you let the jet pour in the dark and watch the light follow the curve.

flow.do: Draw the bottle, the torch and the curved jet. Draw the light inside the jet as a zigzag line that follows the curve. Write one sentence on why the light does not escape.
flow.say: Draw the bottle and the jet. Draw the light as a zigzag inside the jet. Then write why it does not escape.
flow.kid: Draw the jet. Draw a zigzag of light inside it. Write why it stays in.

ask.q: Where does the light finally come out?
good: Where the jet breaks into drops, and where it lands in the sink.
At the splash, where the angle is no longer shallow.
At the end, where the water scatters.

flow.think: A glass fibre does the same thing as the jet. What could you send along it?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the jet and the zigzag of light and explain why the light stays inside.

projects.title: Two-Lens Telescope: see faraway things upside down

materials.item: a weak bulging lens: reading spectacles with a power of plus 2 to plus 3 (a focal length of 50 to 33 centimetres), which you can borrow or buy for about Rs 100 to 200. You use the whole spectacle front
a strong hand lens or a magnifier, about 5 to 10 centimetres focal length, such as a 5 times or 10 times reading magnifier

two tubes that slide into each other, easiest made by rolling A3 chart paper or a thin cereal-box card into tubes and taping them: one about 8 centimetres wide and 40 centimetres long, and one a little thinner and 40 centimetres long
strong tape, black paper or a black marker, scissors and modelling clay (or a small ball of flour dough)
a ruler or tape measure, a white card and a bright window

schedule.what: Find the focal length of each lens. Build the tube. Slide it to focus on a far signboard. Work out how many times it magnifies.

projects.record: A drawing of the telescope with the two lenses labelled. The two focal lengths in centimetres, the length of the tube, and how many times you think it magnifies. A sentence on why things look upside down.
projects.safety: Never look at the Sun through the telescope or the lenses. It can blind. Keep lenses out of direct sunlight, because they can start fires. A grown-up helps with the scissors. Borrowed spectacles belong to someone: tape only the card ring, not the lens.
projects.context: In this project, you build a telescope from two lenses, and a tube made from card. You find how much it magnifies, and why the picture is upside down.

setup.art: A pair of reading spectacles held in front of a bright window, throwing a small upside-down picture of the window onto a white card, with a ruler measuring the distance.
setup.caption: 1. Find the focal length of the weak lens with a window and a card.

setup.art: A strong hand magnifier held close to a printed page, with its focal length marked on a ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Find the focal length of the strong lens by finding its sharp picture of the window.

setup.art: Two card tubes, one sliding inside the other, with the weak lens taped at the front of the big tube and the strong lens taped at the far end of the thin tube.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the weak lens to the big tube and the strong lens to the thin tube.

setup.art: A child looking through the tube at a faraway signboard, which appears upside down and bigger, with her other hand sliding the thin tube in and out.
setup.caption: 4. Look at a far signboard and slide the tubes to focus.

flow.do: Show your child the two lenses and the card tubes. Ask for a guess about what the telescope will show, and which way up. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will make a telescope from two lenses. What do you think we will see when we look at something faraway? Will it be bigger? Which way up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two lenses make a telescope. Will it show things bigger? Which way up?

ask.q: Why do you think two lenses might be better than one?
good: One lens makes a picture, and the other makes it bigger.
Two lenses bend the light twice.
They work together, like a team.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one finds each lens's focal length, the other builds the tube; then each takes a turn at the eyepiece. Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Lens Telescope project. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Hold the reading spectacles with one lens toward a bright window about 4 metres away. Hold the white card behind the lens and slide it to find the sharpest small picture of the window. Measure the distance from the lens to the card in centimetres. This is the focal length of the weak lens. Write it down.
flow.say: Hold the weak lens toward the window. Slide the white card behind it until a small picture of the window is sharp. Measure the distance. That is the focal length of this lens.
flow.kid: Hold the lens at the window. Slide the card. Measure where the picture is sharp.
flow.parent: A weak lens has a long focal length, such as 50 centimetres or more. The picture will be tiny and upside down. Write the focal length down. You will use it to cut the tube and to work out the magnification.
flow.context: In this step, you find the focal length of the weak lens.

flow.do: Do the same with the strong hand lens. Hold it toward the window and slide the card behind it, close to the lens. Measure the distance for the sharpest picture. This is the focal length of the strong lens. Write it down.
flow.say: Now the strong lens. Hold it at the window and slide the card close behind. Measure the distance. This focal length should be much shorter.
flow.kid: Do the same with the strong lens. Measure where the picture is sharp.
flow.parent: The strong lens should have a focal length of about 5 to 10 centimetres. If it is much longer than 15 centimetres, the telescope will not magnify much. Find a stronger lens, or hold two bulging lenses from old reading glasses together.
flow.context: In this step, you find the focal length of the strong lens.

flow.do: A grown-up helps cut the card. Cut a card ring so one spectacle lens shows through it. Tape the ring, with the lens centred over the opening, to one end of the wider tube. Cover the other spectacle lens with black card. Tape the strong lens to one end of the thinner tube. Slide the thin tube into the wide tube, so that the lenses face outward at the two ends. Check that the tubes slide in and out smoothly. Paint or colour the inside black.
flow.say: Tape the weak lens to the wide tube. Tape the strong lens to the thin tube. Slide one tube inside the other. The lenses face outward at the two ends.
flow.kid: Tape the weak lens to the big tube. Tape the strong lens to the thin tube.
flow.parent: The weak lens goes at the front, and the strong lens is the eyepiece. If you swap them, you get a poor telescope. Blackening the inside with a marker cuts the stray light. The tubes should slide back and forth by about the focal length of the strong lens. When fully out, the tube should be about as long as the two focal lengths added together (about 58 centimetres for 50 and 8 centimetres). Expect a rough, dim, colour-fringed picture; it is a model that works, not a good telescope.

check.q: Which lens goes at the front of the telescope, facing the faraway thing?
options: The weak lens with the long focal length
The strong lens with the short focal length
check.why: The front lens makes a small picture of the faraway thing, and the strong eyepiece magnifies that picture. If you swap them, the weak lens would have to magnify a tiny picture, which it cannot do well. A hollow lens in front would only spread the light out.

flow.context: In this step, you build the telescope from two lenses and two card tubes.

flow.do: Take the telescope to a window or a terrace. Look through the strong lens at a signboard or a tree 50 metres away or more. Slide the thin tube in and out until the picture is sharp. Look at how big and which way up the picture is. Never point it at the Sun.
flow.say: Look through the strong lens at a far signboard. Slide the tube in and out. When the picture is sharp, tell me what you see. Which way up is it?
flow.kid: Look through the small lens at a far sign. Slide the tube. What do you see?

ask.q: Which way up is the picture? Why do you think that is?
good: It is upside down, because the first lens crosses the rays over.
The lens makes an upside-down picture, and the eyepiece does not turn it back.
It is upside down, like the picture on the card.

flow.parent: The picture will look upside down. This is correct for this kind of telescope. If it is blurry, slide the tube further. If you see colour fringes, that is normal for a simple lens. If the picture stays blurry at every position, check that the two focal lengths are right, and hold the tube against a wall or a window frame to keep it steady. Typical magnification is only about 4 to 8 times. Choose a far sign, a tree or a building to look at. Do not look at the Sun, ever.
flow.context: In this step, you use the telescope to look at something far away.

flow.do: Work out how much your telescope magnifies, by dividing the weak lens's focal length by the strong lens's focal length. Check by looking at a row of bricks or tiles with one eye through the telescope and the other eye bare. Count how many bricks seen with the bare eye fit in one brick seen through the telescope.
flow.say: Divide the weak lens's focal length by the strong lens's focal length. That is how many times it magnifies. Then check with a wall of bricks.
flow.kid: Divide the long focal length by the short one. That is the magnification.

ask.q: Does the number you counted match the number you worked out?
good: It is close, but not exactly the same.
Yes. My telescope magnifies about 6 times.
No, because it is hard to count with one eye in each place.

flow.parent: A weak lens of 50 centimetres and a strong lens of 8 centimetres gives about 6 times. The bricks test is difficult, so a result within a factor of one and a half is good. If the numbers are far apart, check the two focal lengths again.
flow.context: In this step, you work out how much your telescope magnifies, and check it by counting.

challenges.title: Bottle Bulb: light a dark box with a bottle of water
challenges.problem: A small storeroom with no window stays dark in the daytime. Make a model of it from a shoebox with a closed lid. Use a clear bottle of water and the Sun to light up the inside, so that you can read a line of print in the far corner.
constraints: Use only sunlight. No lamp, no torch and no mirror.
Use one clear plastic bottle full of water. Do not add any chemicals.
The lid of the shoebox must stay closed. The only way for light in is through the bottle.
You must be able to read a line of print, in the far corner of the box, from outside, through a small viewing hole.
materials: a shoebox with a lid, painted black inside or lined with black paper
a clear plastic bottle of about 500 millilitres, with its label removed, full of water, with the cap on tight
scissors, strong tape and thick black paper
a printed line of text in large letters, taped to the far inside corner of the box
a sunny window, balcony or terrace
general: A plain water-filled bottle pushed halfway into a round hole in the lid, with the neck outside in the sun.
A bottle with a piece of black paper wrapped around the part outside the box, leaving only the top open to the sun, so that light goes mostly down into the bottle.
A bottle fixed so that its middle is level with the lid, and tape sealing the gaps around it so no stray light gets in.
creative: Add two or three drops of milk to the water, which scatters the light more widely inside the box.
Use two bottles in two holes, one over each end of the box.
Cover the part of the bottle inside the box with a strip of frosted tape, which makes a softer, wider glow.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it in the sun. How well can you read the print in the far corner? Change one thing, such as adding milk, and test again. Which design lit the box best? Why do you think it did? Does it light the whole box evenly, or just one bright spot?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about using bent light. Real people in homes without windows have used water-filled bottles through the roof to bring daylight in, and you make a model.

setup.art: A child sketching three designs for a bottle in a shoebox lid: a plain bottle, a bottle wrapped in black paper, and two bottles.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: A shoebox with a bottle of water pushed halfway through a round hole in the lid, standing in bright sunlight on a windowsill, with a small viewing hole on the side.
setup.caption: 2. Build the box. Put the bottle in the hole, and put the box in the Sun.

setup.art: A child looking through the small viewing hole at a line of print in the far corner lit by a soft glow from the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Look through the viewing hole. Can you read the print?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three different ways to put the bottle into the lid. Ask what the water will do to the sunlight.
flow.say: A room with no window stays dark. You have a bottle of water and some sunlight. How could the bottle bring light inside? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: A dark box. A bottle of water. Sunlight. Draw ideas for bringing light in.

ask.q: What do you think the water will do to the sunlight?
good: It will bend the light.
It will spread the light out inside the box.
The water will act like a big lens.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Bulb challenge. You plan.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a round hole in the lid, a little smaller than the bottle. Push the bottle halfway into the hole, so that the neck points out and up. Tape around the bottle where it meets the lid, so that no light leaks in. Cut a small viewing hole in the side of the box, near the far corner. Tape a line of large print in the far corner inside.
flow.say: Cut a hole in the lid and push the bottle into it, halfway. Seal the gap with tape. Then make a small viewing hole in the side. Tape the print in the far corner.
flow.kid: Cut a round hole in the lid. Push the bottle in halfway. Seal it with tape.
flow.parent: Make the hole a bit smaller than the bottle, so it sits tight. Scissors can slip on a hard lid, so a grown-up should cut it. Black paper inside the box stops the light from bouncing about and makes the result clearer. Keep the first design simple, so you have something to beat.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design.

flow.do: Take the box to a sunny window, balcony or terrace, with the bottle on top. Water in a bottle can focus sunlight like a lens. Keep paper, cloth and skin away from the bright spot. Never look at the Sun through it. Look through the viewing hole, and try to read the print in the far corner. Note how bright the box looks inside. Compare with a plain round hole of the same size in a second lid, if you have time.
flow.say: Put the box in the Sun. Look in through the little hole. Can you read the print in the far corner? How bright is the inside? Is the light a spot or all over?
flow.kid: Put the box in the Sun. Look in. Can you read the print?

ask.q: Is the bottle lighting the whole box, or just one bright spot?
good: The whole box glows softly.
The light spreads out from the bottle.
A plain hole makes one bright spot, but the bottle spreads the light out.

flow.parent: A plain hole makes a bright spot of sunlight, but leaves the rest dark. The bottle bends the light and spreads it widely, so the whole box glows. This is the idea behind the real bottle lights people have fitted through roofs. If the box looks dark, check for gaps in the tape, and try a brighter, sunnier place.
flow.context: In this step, you test your design in the Sun.

flow.do: Change one thing. You could add two drops of milk to the water. Or wrap black paper round the top of the bottle. Test again. Write down which design lit the print best, and why you think so.
flow.say: Change one thing. Test it again. Was the print easier or harder to read? Which design is the best so far, and why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which is best?

ask.q: Which change made the biggest difference, and why do you think so?
good: Milk made the light more even, because it scatters the light.
Sealing the gaps made it darker, which helped me see the light.
The black paper kept the extra light out, so the glow was clearer.

flow.context: In this step, you improve your design by changing one thing.

items.p: In a drawing of light bending at a water surface, what is the normal?
opts: An imaginary line standing at a right angle to the surface, at the spot where the light arrives
The flat surface of the water
The path of the light in the water
items.why: Scientists measure every bend from the normal, the upright line at a right angle to the surface. Choosing the surface is a common mistake, and it gives the wrong angles. A beam along the normal has an angle of 0 degrees.

items.p: When light goes at a slant from air into water, it bends ____ the normal.
items.why: Light moves more slowly in water, so it bends toward the normal. The angle in the water is smaller than the angle in the air.

items.p: True or false: a torch beam that arrives along the normal into water bends a lot.
items.a: False
items.why: False. Light that arrives along the normal does not bend at all. The bend only happens when the light arrives at a slant.

items.p: A torch beam goes into a tank of water at 50 degrees from the normal. Which angle in the water is the most likely?
items.why: The water turns the beam toward the normal, so the angle in the water must be smaller than 50 degrees. It is about 35 degrees. Choosing 20 degrees bends the beam too much. Choosing 65 degrees bends it the wrong way.

items.p: Put the steps of the Measure the Bend experiment in order, from first to last.
items: Draw the surface line and the normal at the point O
Draw lines at 20, 40 and 60 degrees from the normal
Lay the torch at the end of a line, aimed at O
Mark two dots on the bright line that leaves the far wall of the box
Join O to the wall point and measure its angle from the normal
items.why: First draw the map with the normal, so that every angle has a place to be measured from. Then place the torch, find where the beam leaves, and measure. Without the normal drawn first, the angles have nothing to be measured from.

items.p: Sort these journeys of light. Does the light bend toward the normal, bend away from it, or not bend?
items: air into water at a slant
Bends toward the normal
water into air at a slant
Bends away from the normal
air into glass at a slant
Bends toward the normal
glass into air at a slant
Bends away from the normal
a beam along the normal into water
Does not bend
a beam across a room of still air
Does not bend
items.a: see items
items.why: Light bends toward the normal when it goes into a material that is slower, such as water or glass. It bends away when it goes into a faster material, such as air. Light that goes along the normal, or stays in one material, does not bend.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: normal
the imaginary upright line at a right angle to a surface
refractive index
a number telling how many times slower light is in a material
critical angle
the angle beyond which light inside a material is trapped
optical fibre
a hair-thin glass strand that carries light by trapping it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The normal is the line we measure from. The refractive index is a number for how much a material slows light. The critical angle tells us when light is trapped, and a fibre is the thing that uses that to carry light.

items.p: Water, glass, air and diamond all slow light. Which slows it the most?
items.why: Diamond has a refractive index of about 2.4, the biggest of these. Light in diamond moves at less than half its speed in air. Glass is about 1.5, water about 1.33, and air is almost 1.

items.p: True or false: cooking oil floats on water, so it bends light less than water does.
items.a: False
items.why: False. Oil is lighter than water for its size, yet it bends light more. The bend depends on how the atoms of a material react to light, and not on how heavy the material is.

items.p: The bigger the refractive index of a material, the ____ light moves through it.
items.why: The refractive index tells how many times slower light is in a material than in empty space. A bigger number means slower light and a bigger bend.

items.p: When can light inside water be trapped by the surface?
opts: When it reaches the surface at a very shallow angle, beyond about 49 degrees from the normal
When it reaches the surface along the normal
When the water is very deep
items.why: Trapping, or total internal reflection, happens only when the angle from the normal is bigger than the critical angle, which is about 49 degrees for water. Light along the normal goes straight out. Depth and temperature do not matter much.

items.p: The top of the water in a glass can look like a window from one place and a mirror from another. Explain how one surface can be both.
items.a: The water is the same, but the angle of the light is different. At a steep angle, light from below passes through the top, so it is a window. At a shallow angle, bigger than about 49 degrees from the normal, no light can get out, so it all bounces back, and the top is a mirror.
items.why: A strong answer says that the angle decides, and mentions that beyond the critical angle all the light bounces back. It does not say the water changes.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a ray going from air into water. Label the four parts.
a: the surface of the water: the flat line the ray crosses
the normal: the dotted line at a right angle to the surface
the angle in the air: between the ray in the air and the normal
the angle in the water: between the ray in the water and the normal, and smaller than the angle in the air
items.why: Every bend diagram has the same four parts. The two angles are both measured from the normal. In water, the angle is smaller because the ray bends toward the normal.
items.art: A ray coming from the upper left to a water surface, a dotted normal standing straight up, and the ray bending toward the normal below the surface, with four empty label boxes.

items.p: Draw a ray going at a slant into a glass block, through it, and out the other side. Draw the normal at both surfaces. Show how the ray bends.
items.a: The ray bends toward the normal going in, goes straight in the glass, and bends away from the normal coming out. It leaves parallel to the way it came in, but shifted sideways.
items.why: A strong drawing has a normal at each surface, a bend toward the normal on the way in, and an equal bend away on the way out. The two outside rays are parallel.

items.p: On a hot afternoon, three children look along a road and see a shiny patch that looks like water.

views.says: It is water that someone spilled on the road. That is why it shines.
It is a picture of the sky. Light from the sky bends in the hot air and comes up to our eyes.
It is not there at all. It is a trick of the mind, because our eyes get tired.

items.ask: Which child would you trust most? Give a reason from what you know about light, and say one thing that you would test.
items.a: A strong answer picks the second child, and says that a camera can photograph a mirage, and that the patch moves away as we walk toward it, so it is not real water. Hot air bends light, so a picture of the sky appears on the road. A good test is to take a photo.
items.why: The mirage is made of real light that has been bent by layers of air. A camera sees it, so it is not only in the mind. It is not water, because it keeps moving away and does not wet the road.

items.p: A lens has a focal length of 25 centimetres, which is a quarter of a metre. Its power in dioptres is 1 divided by the focal length in metres. What is its power?
items.why: A quarter of a metre is 0.25 metres. 1 divided by 0.25 is 4. So the lens is 4 dioptres. A shorter focal length means a stronger lens.

worksheets.title: Why Light Bends and Gets Trapped (stretch)

items.p: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres every second in empty space. Glass has a refractive index of about 1.5. About how fast does light go in glass?
items.why: The refractive index says how many times slower light is. 300,000 divided by 1.5 is 200,000. Choosing 450,000 multiplies, which would make light faster in glass. Light never speeds up when it goes into glass.

items.p: A beam goes from air into water at 60 degrees from the normal and bends to 41 degrees from the normal. By how many degrees has the water turned the beam?
items.why: The beam was at 60 degrees in the air and is at 41 degrees in the water. 60 take away 41 is 19. So the water turned the beam by 19 degrees, toward the normal.

items.p: A glass marble almost vanishes in honey. A diamond of the same size would not. What is the best reason?
opts: Honey bends light almost as much as glass does, but much less than diamond does
items.why: We see a clear thing only where light bends or bounces at its edge. Honey and glass slow light by almost the same amount, so there is hardly any bend and the marble nearly vanishes. Diamond slows light far more than honey, so its edge still bends the light a lot.

items.p: True or false: a block of glass with parallel sides turns a beam of light for good.
items.a: False
items.why: False. The ray bends toward the normal going in, and by the same amount away from it coming out, so it leaves going the same way as before, only shifted sideways. A prism, whose sides are not parallel, turns a beam for good.

items.p: After a ray crosses a glass block, it leaves parallel to how it came in, but it has been ____ sideways.
items.why: The two bends cancel, so the direction is the same. But the ray travelled a slanted path inside the glass, so it comes out a little to one side.

items.p: The critical angle is about 42 degrees for glass and about 24 degrees for diamond. Which traps light more easily?
opts: Diamond, because it has the smaller critical angle
Glass, because it has the bigger critical angle
items.why: Light is trapped whenever it meets the edge at an angle bigger than the critical angle. A smaller critical angle means that more of the angles trap light. That is part of why diamonds sparkle.

items.p: Light is going from one material to another at a very shallow angle. In which journeys can it be trapped?
items: from water into air
Can be trapped
from glass into air
Can be trapped
from diamond into air
Can be trapped
from air into water
Cannot be trapped
from air into glass
Cannot be trapped
from water into glass
Cannot be trapped
items.a: see items
items.why: Light can be trapped only when it is going from a slower material to a faster one, because only then does it bend away from the normal so much that it cannot leave. Going into a slower material, the light always bends toward the normal and gets in.

items.p: Put the path of a ray of sunlight through a raindrop in order, from first to last.
items: The ray enters the front of the drop and bends
The ray travels across the drop to the back
The ray bounces off the back of the drop
The ray leaves the front of the drop and bends again
items.why: A rainbow is made by one bend on the way in, one bounce at the back and one bend on the way out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the colours leave in slightly different directions.

items.p: Match each eye or lens problem to what helps.
pairs: short sight, where the picture forms in front of the retina
a hollow lens
long sight, where the picture would form behind the retina
a bulging lens
a faraway thing made big in a telescope
a weak lens in front and a strong lens as the eyepiece
a door peephole showing a small, wide view
a hollow lens
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A hollow lens spreads light, so it moves the picture back and makes things look smaller. A bulging lens bends light more and moves the picture closer. A telescope uses a weak lens to make a small picture and a strong lens to magnify it.

items.p: You walk toward the shiny patch on a hot road, but it keeps moving away. What is the best explanation?
opts: It is a picture of the sky, visible only at a shallow angle, and the angle never changes as you move on
The road dries as you come near
items.why: You see the picture only when you look along the road at a shallow angle. As you walk, a new patch farther ahead meets that same shallow angle. The picture is real light, but it is not a place that you can walk to.

items.p: A fish looks up from under the water. Explain, using the words critical angle, why the fish sees the whole sky in a round window.
items.a: Light from the whole sky bends down into the water at the surface, so all of it is squeezed into a cone about 97 degrees wide above the fish. Outside that cone, the fish sees the underside of the surface at angles bigger than the critical angle of about 49 degrees, where it is a mirror. So the sky fits in a round window, with a silver ring around it.
items.why: A strong answer says that light from every direction of the sky bends into a cone, that the cone is limited by the critical angle, and that beyond it the surface is a mirror.

items.p: Draw a curved optical fibre and show how a ray of light stays inside it. Mark one place where the ray bounces.
items.a: A curved strip with a zigzag line inside it, touching the wall at shallow angles and bouncing off, with no light leaving the strip.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ray hitting the wall at a shallow angle each time and bouncing, with the angle in equal to the angle out. The light follows the curve by many small bounces.

items.p: Two people in a family argue about spectacles for a child who cannot read the board.

views.says: Wearing spectacles will make her eyes weaker, so she should wait as long as she can.
The right spectacles bring the board into focus. She needs them now to learn well.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from what you know about how spectacles work, and say what you would check first.
items.a: A strong answer agrees that the right spectacles bring the picture into focus on the retina, and do not weaken the eyes. Studies do not show harm from the right spectacles. A good first step is an eye test, to find out what lens is needed.
items.why: Spectacles move the picture to the right place on the retina. The eyeball grows with the child, so the lens may need to change, but the spectacles do not weaken the eye.

items.p: A telescope has a weak lens with a focal length of 60 centimetres and a strong eyepiece with a focal length of 6 centimetres. How many times does it magnify?
items.why: A telescope magnifies by the focal length of the first lens divided by the focal length of the eyepiece. 60 divided by 6 is 10. Choosing 54 or 66 adds or subtracts the lengths instead of dividing.

items.p: Here is a drawing of the model eye from the experiment Build an Eye That Needs Spectacles. Label four parts with what they stand for.
a: the magnifying glass: the lens of the eye
the bright window: the faraway thing you look at
the spectacle lens in front: the spectacles that fix the picture
items.why: The model eye works like a real eye. The magnifying glass bends the light, the card is where the picture must come to a sharp point, and the spectacle lens moves the sharp point to the right place.
items.art: A side view of a magnifying glass, a white card behind it, a bright window far to the left, and a spectacle lens held in front, with four empty label boxes.

items.p: Three of these use total internal reflection. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: An optical fibre in a cable
The silver underside of a water surface seen from below
The sparkle of a cut diamond
A magnifying glass making print look bigger
items.why: A magnifying glass makes print look bigger by bending light as it passes through, which is refraction. The fibre, the silver water and the diamond all depend on light being trapped and bounced back inside.

items.p: A ray goes at a slant through a pane of glass. Which pane shifts the ray sideways more: a thin pane or a thick pane?
opts: The thick pane, because the ray travels further on its slanted path inside
Neither, because the ray does not shift
items.why: Inside the glass the ray travels along a slanted line. The longer that path, the further the ray has moved to one side by the time it comes out. A thin pane shifts a ray hardly at all.

items.p: Light travels at about 200,000 kilometres a second in glass. A fibre in a cable is 3,000 kilometres long. How many thousandths of a second does the light take to cross it?
items.why: 3,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.015 of a second, which is 15 thousandths of a second. So light crosses a 3,000 kilometre cable in about 15 thousandths of a second. That is why a call crosses the sea so fast.

items.p: Why can light going from air into water never be trapped by total internal reflection?
opts: It bends toward the normal, so it always gets in
items.why: Going into a slower material, light bends toward the normal, so the angle in the water is always smaller than the angle in the air. It can always get in. Trapping is possible only when light tries to go out into a faster material.

items.p: A diamond cutter makes the sides of a stone at the wrong angles. The diamond looks dull and glassy. Explain why, using the idea of trapped light.
items.a: A diamond sparkles when light that enters the top bounces off the sides inside and comes back out through the top. If the sides are cut at the wrong angle, the light meets them at an angle smaller than the critical angle, so it leaks out through the bottom and never comes back to the eye. So the stone looks dull.
items.why: A strong answer says that light must meet the sides beyond the critical angle to be trapped and sent back. Wrong angles let it leak out the bottom.

items.p: True or false: a hollow lens can throw a sharp picture of a window onto a card.
items.a: False
items.why: False. A hollow lens spreads the rays apart, so they never meet at a point. It can make things look smaller when you look through it, but it cannot throw a picture on a card.

items.p: A lens has a power of 2 dioptres. What is its focal length?
items.why: The power is 1 divided by the focal length in metres. So the focal length is 1 divided by 2, which is half a metre, or 50 centimetres. Choosing 200 centimetres divides the other way round.

items.p: The strength of a lens is measured in a unit called the ____.
items.why: The dioptre is the unit for the power of a lens. A lens of 1 dioptre has a focal length of 1 metre, and a lens of 4 dioptres has a focal length of a quarter of a metre.

items.p: Is the water or glass surface acting like a window or like a mirror?
items: looking straight up at the underside of water
Window, light passes through
looking up at a low slant at the underside of water
Mirror, light is bounced back
light zigzagging along a glass fibre
Mirror, light is bounced back
light going from air into a glass block along the normal
Window, light passes through
items.a: see items
items.why: The same kind of surface does one or the other depending on the angle. Along the normal, light passes through. At a shallow angle from inside a slow material, all of it is bounced back.

items.p: Three people in a class talk about who should get the credit for the telescope.

views.says: Galileo made the first telescope, because he made the discoveries with it.
Lipperhey asked for a patent in 1608, so he was first.
Historians cannot be sure who made the first one, because the earliest records are only patent applications.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, and say what other evidence you would want to see before you decide.
items.a: A strong answer sees that making something first and using it first for discovery are different, and that a patent application is only a record that someone asked. It might ask for older letters, drawings, or lenses made before 1608.
items.why: The first records of a telescope are patent requests from 1608. Others may have made one earlier. Galileo improved the telescope and used it brilliantly, but he did not invent it.

items.p: Put the journey of the light from a faraway tree through a two-lens telescope in order.
items: Light from the tree enters the weak front lens
The front lens makes a small upside-down picture of the tree inside the tube
The strong eyepiece magnifies that small picture
The eye sees a big upside-down tree
items.why: The weak lens makes a small picture first. Then the strong lens acts as a magnifier on that picture. The picture is upside down all the way through, because nothing turns it back.

items.p: Draw a telescope from the side with its two lenses. Show how light from the top of a faraway tree crosses over inside the tube, so that the picture of the tree is upside down.
items.a: A tube with a big lens at the front and a small lens at the eye end. Rays from the top of the tree cross inside, so the top of the tree appears at the bottom of the picture.
items.why: A strong drawing shows rays from the top of the tree crossing over in the tube. That is why the picture ends up upside down.

items.p: A friend says that a mirage is just in your head. Use one fact about cameras to answer.
items.a: A camera can photograph a mirage. So the shiny patch is made of real light that was bent by layers of hot air. What is wrong is the guess that the light came from water on the road.
items.why: A strong answer uses the camera fact and says that the light is real. What is mistaken is the idea of where it came from.

items.p: Which fact shows that a material that is heavier for its size does not always bend light more?
opts: Cooking oil floats on water but bends light more than water does
Glass bends light more than water
items.why: If heavier meant more bending, oil would bend light less than water, because it floats. It bends light more. So the bend does not depend on how heavy the material is for its size.

items.p: Match each strange sight to the reason for it.
pairs: stripes wobble above a hot plate
hot air rising bends light by changing amounts
a glass marble nearly vanishes in honey
honey and glass bend light by almost the same amount
a jet of water glows along its curve
light is trapped inside by total internal reflection
colours in a rainbow
bending and bouncing inside raindrops
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All four are the same bending rule showing up in different places. Which one you see depends on the materials and the angle of the light.

items.p: A telescope has a front lens with a focal length of 90 centimetres and an eyepiece with a focal length of 5 centimetres. How many times does it magnify?
items.why: A telescope magnifies by the focal length of the first lens divided by the focal length of the eyepiece. 90 divided by 5 is 18. So it magnifies 18 times.

items.p: A diver is 4 metres under the sea. The round window of sky above her is about 9 metres wide for every 4 metres of depth. About how wide is it for her?
items.why: She is exactly 4 metres deep, so the window is about 9 metres wide. If she rose to 2 metres, it would be about half as wide, 4 and a half metres. Choosing 36 multiplies the two numbers together.

quiz.p: A ray inside a block of glass goes out into the air at a slant. Which way does it bend?
quiz.why: Light speeds up going from glass into air, so it bends away from the normal. Choosing toward the normal is the rule for going into glass, not out of it.

quiz.p: A beam of light arrives at the surface of a pond exactly along the normal. What does it do?
quiz.why: Light arriving along the normal has an angle of 0 degrees, and it does not bend. The bend appears only when the light arrives at a slant.

quiz.p: What is the main reason light bends when it goes into glass at a slant?
opts: It moves more slowly in glass than in air
quiz.why: Light moves more slowly in glass, and the side of the beam that gets in first slows first, so the beam turns. Pulling, weight and tiredness are common guesses, but none of them is the reason.

quiz.p: Which statement about the refractive index is true?
opts: A bigger number means slower light and a bigger bend
A bigger number means faster light
It tells how heavy a material is
It is the same for every material
quiz.why: The refractive index tells how many times slower light is in a material than in empty space. A bigger number means a bigger slowing and a bigger bend.

quiz.p: A diver on a calm day looks up and sees a bright round window of sky with a silver ring around it. What is the silver ring?
opts: The underside of the water surface acting as a mirror
quiz.why: At shallow angles, light from below meets the surface beyond the critical angle, so all of it bounces back. The ring is a mirror that shows the sea bed. Foam and clouds are not the cause.

quiz.p: What must be true for total internal reflection to happen?
opts: Light goes from a slower material to a faster one, at an angle bigger than the critical angle
Light goes from air into water
quiz.why: Only light trying to leave a slower material for a faster one can be trapped, and only if its angle is bigger than the critical angle. Going into a slower material, light always gets in.

quiz.p: How does an optical fibre keep light inside it as it curves?
opts: The light bounces off the walls again and again, because it meets them at shallow angles
The light is pushed along by wind
The fibre soaks up the light
quiz.why: In a fibre, the light meets the wall at a shallow angle, so total internal reflection sends it back in each time. The light zigzags along, even round curves.

quiz.p: Why does the shiny patch on a hot road seem to move away as you walk toward it?
opts: You see it only along a shallow angle, and ahead of you there is always a new place with that shallow angle
quiz.why: The picture of the sky is seen only when you look along the road at a shallow angle. A new place farther ahead always has that angle. So it keeps moving ahead of you.

quiz.p: A child's eye makes a sharp picture in front of the retina, so faraway things look blurry. Which lens helps?
quiz.why: A hollow lens spreads the light a little first, so the sharp picture moves back onto the retina. A bulging lens would bend the light even more and make the problem worse.

quiz.p: A telescope has lenses with focal lengths of 40 centimetres and 4 centimetres. About how many times does it magnify?
quiz.why: A telescope magnifies by the focal length of the first lens divided by the focal length of the eyepiece. 40 divided by 4 is 10.

quiz.p: Why can you see a rainbow only when the Sun is behind you?
opts: The drops send each colour back toward the Sun's side, at about 42 degrees from the line pointing away from the Sun
The Sun is too bright in front
Rainbows are made by the eyes
quiz.why: Light enters a raindrop, bounces off the back and comes out going back toward where it came from, at about 42 degrees for red. So the drops that send light to your eyes lie in the direction opposite the Sun.

quiz.p: A scientist takes the back coats off an ox eye and sees a tiny upside-down picture on the back wall of the eye. What does this show?
opts: The lens of the eye bends light to form a picture on the retina
The lens of the eye is the screen that sees
Light comes out of the eye
quiz.why: The picture appears on the retina, at the back, and not in the lens. So the lens only helps to bend light into a picture. The old idea, that the lens is where seeing happens, was wrong.

applications: Optical fibre cables carry phone calls and the internet along the floor of the sea, as flashes of light.
Doctors use bundles of optical fibres in thin tubes to look inside the body without a big operation.
Spectacles and contact lenses use hollow and bulging lenses to put the picture on the retina.
A cut diamond or a cut-glass bowl is shaped so that trapped light comes back out of the top and sparkles.
Binoculars and periscopes use glass prisms that bounce light by total internal reflection to turn the picture right way up.
Telescopes and microscopes use two or more lenses to make faraway or tiny things look big.
Cameras and phones use several lenses together to make a sharp picture on a sensor.
Eye surgeons replace a cloudy lens, a cataract, with a clear plastic lens.
Lighthouses use a ring-shaped lens that bends the lamp's light into one strong beam.
Bottle bulbs, bottles of water fixed through a roof, bring daylight into homes with no windows.
