open_questions.q: Which is the best picture of why light slows down in glass?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists agree on the numbers for how much light slows, and on the bends it makes. They use more than one picture to explain what happens inside the material, and they do not always agree on which is best.

open_questions.q: Can light be slowed or stopped and used to store information?
open_questions.why_open: Light has been slowed to the speed of a bicycle and even stopped for a short time in a cloud of atoms. Nobody yet knows if this can be made small and cheap enough to be useful.

open_questions.q: Why do more and more children become short-sighted?
open_questions.why_open: Reports say that short sight in children is rising in many places. Studies link it to more time spent on near work and less time outdoors in daylight, but scientists do not yet agree on the whole cause.

open_questions.q: Can a lens be as flat as a sheet of paper?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016, scientists made flat lenses from tiny pillars of material, called metalenses. Early ones worked well for one colour only. Making them work for all colours, cheaply, is still being worked on.

open_questions.q: Some fish and birds hunt across the water's surface. How do they cope with the bend of light?
open_questions.why_open: Some animals seem to correct for the bend very well. Scientists are still studying how much is learned by practice and how much is born in them.

open_questions.q: Who first used a curved piece of glass or crystal to look closely at things?
open_questions.why_open: Ancient polished crystals have been found in several places, and some may have been used as lenses. Historians do not agree on which ones were, and written records are very scarce.

ask_kids: Where in our home can you find a lens? Think of spectacles, a phone camera and a door peephole.
Put a spoon in your glass of water at lunch. Where does the spoon look broken, and from where does it look whole?
Look at the underside of the water in a glass at a low slant. What colour does it turn?
Which of our spectacles are hollow lenses and which are bulging? How can you tell?
Why do you think a diamond ring sparkles more than a plain piece of glass of the same shape?
Look out of a window at a long road on a sunny day. Can you see a shiny patch? What is it really?
If you looked up from the bottom of a well, what do you think you would see?
Why do you think people in a dark room can see light coming along a thin cable?
What would the world look like if you wore a hollow lens all day?
Whose spectacles in our family are the strongest? How could we find out their power?

jokes.j: Why did the ray of light refuse to go straight into the water?
jokes.a: It wanted to take a turn for the better.

jokes.j: Why are bulging lenses such good friends?
Why did the hollow lens feel left out?
jokes.a: Because everyone kept spreading apart from her.

jokes.j: Why did the fish love her round window?
jokes.a: She had a great view of the whole sky.

jokes.j: What do optical fibres eat for lunch?
Why did the mirage never get invited to the party?
jokes.a: Nobody could ever find it when they got there.

jokes.j: What did the glass block say to the ray of light?
jokes.a: Come in, but you will leave a little to the side.

jokes.j: Why did the telescope have two lenses?
jokes.a: One to look at the far, and one to look at the near.

jokes.j: Why did the diamond refuse to let any light go?
jokes.a: It had a strong critical angle.

maths.problem: In the Measure the Bend experiment, a beam meets the water at 30 degrees from the normal. Inside the water it is at 22 degrees from the normal. By how many degrees did the water turn the beam?
maths.explain: The beam was at 30 degrees in the air and at 22 degrees in the water. 30 take away 22 is 8. So the water turned the beam by 8 degrees, toward the normal.
maths.context: In Measure the Bend, you shine a beam into water at different slants and measure the angle in the water.
maths.why_maths: Taking one angle from the other tells you how much the water turned the beam, so you can compare one slant with another.

maths.problem: Light moves at about 300,000 kilometres a second in empty space and at about 225,000 kilometres a second in water. What fraction of its speed does light keep in water?
maths.explain: 225,000 out of 300,000 is the same as 225 out of 300. Divide both by 75 to get 3 out of 4. So light keeps three quarters of its speed in water, which is why water has a refractive index of about 1.33.
maths.context: You learned that light slows down in water and bends toward the normal.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the speed tells you how strong a slowing is, so you can compare water with glass and diamond.

maths.problem: Seen from straight above, a temple tank looks 3 metres deep. Water looks three quarters as deep as it really is. How deep is the tank really?
maths.explain: 3 metres is three quarters of the real depth. One quarter is 3 divided by 3, which is 1 metre. The whole depth is 4 quarters, which is 4 metres. So the tank is 4 metres deep.
maths.context: You learned that light bending out of water makes the bottom look closer than it is.
maths.why_maths: Working backwards from how deep the water looks tells you how deep it really is. Water is always deeper than it looks.

maths.problem: Light moves at about 200,000 kilometres a second in glass. A fibre in a cable under the sea is 3,000 kilometres long. How many thousandths of a second does the light take to travel along it?
maths.explain: Time is distance divided by speed. 3,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.015 of a second. That is 15 thousandths of a second. So a flash of light crosses the whole cable in less than one fiftieth of a second.
maths.context: You learned that optical fibres carry flashes of light between countries along the sea floor.
maths.why_maths: Dividing distance by speed tells you how long a message takes to cross an ocean, and shows why calls across the sea seem instant.

maths.problem: A diver's round window of sky is about 9 metres wide for every 4 metres of depth. How wide is the window for a diver at 8 metres? And for a diver at 2 metres?
maths.answer: 18 metres at 8 metres deep, and 4 and a half metres at 2 metres deep.
maths.explain: 8 metres is two lots of 4 metres, so the window is two lots of 9 metres, which is 18 metres. 2 metres is half of 4 metres, so the window is half of 9 metres, which is 4 and a half metres. The deeper you go, the wider the window.
maths.context: You learned that the window of sky seen from under the water gets smaller as a diver rises.
maths.why_maths: A ratio lets you predict the size of the window at any depth, and shows why it shrinks as you rise.

maths.problem: Reading spectacles marked plus 2 have a focal length of 50 centimetres. A hand magnifier has a focal length of 25 centimetres. Which is stronger, and how many times stronger?
maths.answer: The magnifier is stronger, twice as strong.
maths.explain: A shorter focal length means a stronger lens. 25 centimetres is half of 50 centimetres. The magnifier is 4 dioptres, because 1 divided by a quarter of a metre is 4. The spectacles are 2 dioptres. 4 is twice 2.
maths.context: In Build an Eye That Needs Spectacles and the Two-Lens Telescope, you use lenses with different focal lengths.
maths.why_maths: Comparing focal lengths with numbers tells you which lens is stronger without having to test them.

maths.problem: You want a telescope that magnifies 12 times. The front lens has a focal length of 60 centimetres. What focal length must the eyepiece have?
maths.explain: Magnification is the front focal length divided by the eyepiece focal length. So the eyepiece focal length is 60 divided by 12, which is 5 centimetres. Check: 60 divided by 5 is 12.
maths.context: In the Two-Lens Telescope project, you divide the focal lengths of your two lenses to find how much the telescope magnifies.
maths.why_maths: Working backwards from the magnification you want tells you which eyepiece to look for before you build.

maths.problem: The critical angle is about 49 degrees for water, about 42 degrees for glass and about 24 degrees for diamond. Put them in order, from the one that traps light most easily to the one that traps it least easily. How many degrees apart are water and diamond?
maths.answer: Diamond, then glass, then water. Water and diamond are 25 degrees apart.
maths.explain: A smaller critical angle means that light is trapped at more angles, so diamond traps most easily, then glass, then water. 49 take away 24 is 25 degrees.
maths.context: You learned that light inside a material is trapped when it meets the edge at an angle bigger than the critical angle.
maths.why_maths: Ordering the critical angles tells you which materials make the best sparkle or the best fibre.

maths.problem: A rainbow is a circle around the point exactly opposite the Sun, and the red arc is 42 degrees from that point. That point is as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it. The Sun is 20 degrees above the horizon. How high above the horizon is the top of the rainbow?
maths.explain: The centre of the circle is 20 degrees below the horizon. The top of the rainbow is 42 degrees above the centre. 42 take away 20 is 22 degrees above the horizon. If the Sun were higher than 42 degrees, the whole rainbow would be below the horizon, and we would not see it from the ground.
maths.context: You learned that red light leaves a raindrop at about 42 degrees from the line pointing away from the Sun.
maths.why_maths: Adding and taking away angles tells you where in the sky to look for a rainbow, and why you see none when the Sun is high.

warmup.q: What is the normal in a bend diagram?
warmup.a: An imaginary line at a right angle to the surface. We measure every angle from it.

warmup.q: A beam goes from air into water at a slant. Which way does it bend?
warmup.a: Toward the normal, because light slows down in water.

warmup.q: What does light do when it arrives along the normal?
warmup.a: It goes straight on without bending.

warmup.q: What does a bigger refractive index mean?
warmup.a: Slower light in the material, and a bigger bend.
Light inside a material that bounces back from the edge, because it meets it at a very shallow angle.

warmup.q: Why does a fish see the whole sky in a round window?
warmup.a: The surface bends light from the whole sky into a cone, and beyond it the surface is a mirror.

warmup.q: How does an optical fibre carry light round a bend?
warmup.a: The light bounces off the walls inside again and again.

warmup.q: What is a hollow lens used for?
warmup.a: To fix short sight, because it spreads the light a little before it enters the eye.

warmup.q: How do you find how much a telescope magnifies?
warmup.a: Divide the focal length of the front lens by the focal length of the eyepiece.

quiz: When light goes at a slant into a material where it moves more slowly, it bends toward the normal line.
The normal is a line at right angles to the surface; the beam turns toward it.
Light that arrives straight on, along the normal, does not bend at all.
Both sides of the beam slow at the same time, so it does not turn.
A denser material always bends light more than a lighter one.
Oil is lighter than water yet bends light more; what matters is how much it slows light.
Light inside water, hitting the surface at a very shallow angle, can all bounce back.
This is total internal reflection; none of the light gets out.
The silver ceiling under water is a mirror coating that the water makes.
No coating exists; it happens only where light meets the surface at a shallow angle.
A mirage on a hot road is only a trick of the mind.
A camera can photograph it; the light has really been bent by hot air.
Optical fibres carry light along their length by trapping it inside.
Light keeps bouncing off the inside wall of the glass strand, even round bends.
All lenses make things look bigger.
A hollow lens spreads light out and makes things look smaller.
In short sight, the eye bends light too much, so the picture forms before the retina.
Hollow spectacles spread the light a little first, which moves the picture back onto the retina.
Wearing the right spectacles makes your eyes weaker.
Studies do not show this; short sight often changes as the eyeball grows.
odd: The first three slow light and bend it toward the normal; water into air speeds it up and bends it away.
The first three trap light inside by total internal reflection; a window pane lets it pass straight through.
The first three spread light out and make things look smaller; a magnifying glass is a bulging lens.
Spectacles, telescopes and prisms bend light as it passes through glass; a mirror image comes from light bouncing.
In the first three, light bends gradually through air that is hotter in some places than in others; a glass block bends it only at its edges.
